conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.back: If the patient deteriorates with FALLING cell counts (cytopenias), a soaring ferritin, and a paradoxically FALLING ESR against a rising or persistently high CRP (fibrinogen is being consumed) — plus falling fibrinogen, rising triglycerides and deranged LFTs and coagulation. A falling ESR here is NOT improvement.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.front: What is the overarching management principle for AOSD?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.back: NSAIDs → corticosteroids → DMARDs/biologics (especially IL-1 and IL-6 blockade).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.front: What is the first-line treatment of MILD adult-onset Still's disease, and for how long is it trialled?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.back: NSAIDs — for fever, arthralgia and serositis; trialled for at least a week before adding steroids in mild disease. But corticosteroids are started immediately if there is severe systemic, organ-threatening or MAS-associated disease.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.front: Which DMARDs/biologics are used in persistent AOSD?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.back: Methotrexate (steroid-sparing) — ONCE WEEKLY, never daily, with weekly folic acid on a different day and FBC/LFT/U&E monitoring (MHRA). Because AOSD is IL-1/IL-6-driven, IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab) and IL-6 inhibitors (tocilizumab) are particularly effective; anti-TNF is occasionally used but is less effective and has largely been superseded. All carry serious-infection risk: screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before starting and avoid live vaccines — and note that IL-6 blockade suppresses CRP and fever, so it can mask intercurrent infection.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.front: How is macrophage activation syndrome managed?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.back: Urgent high-dose corticosteroids (e.g. IV methylprednisolone) with or without ciclosporin or anakinra, and immediate rheumatology and haematology input — this is a medical emergency.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the three types of muscle, and what unites them?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle — all generate force by the same fundamental actin-myosin (sliding-filament) mechanism, triggered by calcium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Along what three axes do the three muscle types differ?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Control (voluntary vs involuntary), structure (striated vs not), and behaviour (fast/fatiguing vs rhythmic/tireless vs slow/sustained).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the main job of each of the three muscle types?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Skeletal = voluntary movement/posture; cardiac = pumping blood (rhythmic, tireless); smooth = moving contents through hollow organs (sustained, involuntary).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Describe the control, striation and nuclei of SKELETAL muscle.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Voluntary (somatic NS), striated, and multinucleate.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Describe the control, striation and nuclei of CARDIAC muscle.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary, with one or two central nuclei, branching fibres joined by intercalated discs.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Describe the control, striation and nuclei of SMOOTH muscle.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Involuntary (autonomic), non-striated, with a single nucleus.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How does skeletal muscle behave, and how is its force graded?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It contracts fast and forcefully but fatigues; force is graded by recruitment (more motor units) and frequency (summation → tetanus).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How is skeletal muscle controlled at the cellular level?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Voluntarily, via the somatic nervous system → the neuromuscular junction (ACh acting on nicotinic receptors).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Contrast Type I and Type II skeletal muscle fibres.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Type I (slow-twitch) = slow, sustained, aerobic (mitochondria-rich, red). Type II (fast-twitch) = fast and powerful, mainly glycolytic and quicker to fatigue — type IIa are more oxidative and fatigue-resistant than type IIx.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How do training adaptations relate to muscle fibre types?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Endurance training favours type I adaptations; power training favours type II.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What structural feature electrically couples cardiac muscle cells?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Intercalated discs containing gap junctions → cells are electrically coupled, so the heart contracts as a functional syncytium (all cells fire together).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is automaticity in cardiac muscle?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: The SA node has intrinsic pacemaker activity, so the heart beats without nervous input.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why can cardiac muscle not be tetanised, and why does this matter?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Cardiac muscle has a long refractory period so it cannot be tetanised — essential because the ventricle must relax and refill between beats; a permanently contracted pump ejects nothing.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How does cardiac muscle's calcium handling differ from skeletal?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Cardiac muscle uses Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release and is more dependent on EXTRACELLULAR calcium (extracellular Ca²⁺ triggers release from the SR).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Describe the structure and control of smooth muscle.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Non-striated (actin/myosin arranged differently), spindle-shaped, single-nucleus cells; controlled involuntarily by the autonomic NS, hormones, local factors and stretch.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the 'latch mechanism' of smooth muscle?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: A mechanism allowing slow, sustained contraction at low energy cost — smooth muscle can maintain tone for long periods without fatiguing (e.g. vascular tone, sphincters).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Contrast single-unit and multi-unit smooth muscle.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Single-unit (gap junctions → contracts as a sheet, e.g. gut, bladder, can be spontaneously active) vs multi-unit (individually controlled, e.g. iris, large airways).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How does the calcium mechanism of smooth muscle differ from striated muscle?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Smooth muscle uses CALMODULIN (not troponin) → Ca²⁺-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase → contraction; striated muscle (skeletal/cardiac) uses troponin.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the common contractile mechanism shared by all three muscle types?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Calcium triggers actin and myosin filaments to slide past each other (the sliding-filament mechanism); the differences are only in the details.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the two key detail differences in calcium handling across the muscle types?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Skeletal + cardiac use troponin (striated); smooth uses calmodulin. Skeletal Ca²⁺ comes mostly from the SR, whereas cardiac also needs extracellular Ca²⁺.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Give clinical examples of smooth muscle as a drug target.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: β2-agonists relax airways (asthma), calcium-channel blockers relax vessels (BP), and antimuscarinics relax the bladder.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Name muscle-type-related clinical conditions.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Rhabdomyolysis — muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin (causing AKI), potassium (hyperkalaemia) and CK. Management is aggressive intravenous fluids with urgent potassium, ECG and CK monitoring.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the two stages of muscle contraction?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Excitation-contraction coupling (turning the electrical signal into a calcium release) and the sliding-filament mechanism (using that calcium to make actin and myosin slide past each other) — calcium is the trigger, ATP is the fuel.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the sarcomere?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: The repeating contractile unit of striated (skeletal + cardiac) muscle — its regular arrangement produces the striped appearance.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the thick and thin filaments of the sarcomere?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Thick filaments = myosin (with heads that bind actin — the 'motor'); thin filaments = actin plus the regulatory proteins troponin and tropomyosin.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What do the Z-lines represent in the sarcomere?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: The boundaries of each sarcomere, where the thin (actin) filaments anchor.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the roles of tropomyosin and troponin?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Tropomyosin blocks the actin-myosin binding site at rest; troponin binds calcium → moves tropomyosin out of the way → allows contraction (this is where calcium acts).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the four steps of excitation-contraction coupling?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: (1) An AP arrives (motor neuron → NMJ → ACh → muscle depolarises); (2) the AP spreads inward down the T-tubules; (3) the T-tubule AP triggers the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) to release calcium; (4) calcium binds troponin → moves tropomyosin → exposes actin sites → contraction begins.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the role of the T-tubules?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: They carry the action potential deep into the fibre so calcium is released everywhere at once, giving a uniform contraction.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the role of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It is the calcium store — calcium release from the SR is the trigger for contraction.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How does cardiac excitation-contraction coupling differ?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Cardiac muscle also needs extracellular calcium entering (via the plateau) to trigger SR calcium release — calcium-induced calcium release — so cardiac contraction depends on extracellular Ca²⁺.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What happens in the sliding-filament mechanism once calcium exposes the binding sites?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Myosin heads pull the actin filaments inward → the sarcomere shortens; the filaments SLIDE past each other, they do not shorten themselves.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the four steps of the cross-bridge cycle?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: (1) Cross-bridge formation — the myosin head binds the exposed actin site; (2) power stroke — the myosin head pivots and pulls actin inward (ADP + Pi released); (3) detachment — ATP binds myosin, which releases actin; (4) re-cocking — ATP is hydrolysed and the myosin head re-cocks for the next cycle.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the two essentials for the cross-bridge cycle?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Calcium = the trigger (exposes binding sites via troponin); ATP = the fuel (needed for both the power stroke and detachment).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why does no ATP mean the muscle stays locked?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: ATP is needed for myosin to detach from actin; without ATP the myosin head cannot release, so the muscle stays rigidly contracted (rigor mortis).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How does muscle relaxation occur, and why is it active?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: When the AP stops, calcium is pumped back into the SR by a Ca²⁺-ATPase (using ATP); calcium falls, troponin releases it, tropomyosin re-blocks the sites and the cross-bridges stop — relaxation is active because it needs ATP to pump calcium back.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why does ATP depletion prevent relaxation?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Because relaxation requires ATP to pump calcium back into the SR; without ATP, calcium stays high and myosin stays bound → rigor.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the mechanism of rigor mortis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: After death ATP runs out, so myosin cannot detach from actin (no ATP to release it) → muscles stay rigidly contracted (resolving as proteins decompose) — the classic 'ATP for detachment' illustration.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the mechanism of malignant hyperthermia, and its treatment?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: A genetic RYR1 receptor defect: volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium trigger massive uncontrolled SR calcium release → sustained contraction, hyperthermia, rigidity and rising CO2. Immediate management: stop the trigger and call for help, 100% oxygen with hyperventilation, switch to intravenous anaesthesia, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenously repeated to a maximum of 10 mg/kg, active cooling, and treat hyperkalaemia and acidosis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What causes muscle fatigue at the mechanistic level?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Reduced ATP, impaired calcium handling and accumulation of metabolites → reduced force.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the role of dystrophin, and its clinical relevance?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Dystrophin is a structural protein linking the sarcomere to the membrane; a defect causes muscle damage — as in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How does dantrolene work?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It blocks SR calcium release — used in malignant hyperthermia (and spasticity).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the neuromuscular junction (NMJ)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: The specialised chemical synapse where a motor neuron meets a skeletal muscle fibre — where the nervous system's command becomes muscle contraction, using acetylcholine (ACh) acting on nicotinic receptors.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the three structural parts of the NMJ?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: A presynaptic terminal (motor nerve ending), a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic membrane (the muscle's motor end plate, folded to pack in receptors).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the steps of transmission at the NMJ?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: (1) AP arrives at the nerve terminal; (2) voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ enters; (3) Ca²⁺ triggers vesicles to release ACh; (4) ACh binds nicotinic receptors → depolarisation (end-plate potential); (5) this triggers a muscle AP → contraction; (6) acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh to stop the signal.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What terminates the signal at the NMJ?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down ACh in the synaptic cleft.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the 'safety margin' of the NMJ, and why does it matter?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Far more ACh is released than needed, so one nerve AP reliably triggers one muscle AP (unlike CNS synapses needing summation); NMJ diseases work by eroding this safety margin.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the two key molecular players at the NMJ that are drug/disease targets?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: The nicotinic ACh receptors (postsynaptic) and acetylcholinesterase (which terminates the signal).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the defect and clinical pattern in myasthenia gravis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Antibodies against the postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptor → fewer working receptors → fatigable weakness that worsens with use. Associated with thymoma in a minority (about 10-15%); thymic hyperplasia is commoner, and some patients are anti-MuSK positive rather than anti-AChR.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the defect and clinical pattern in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels → reduced ACh release → weakness that IMPROVES with use. Paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer) in about half of cases.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How do myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton syndrome differ?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Myasthenia = postsynaptic (receptor), worsens with use; Lambert-Eaton = presynaptic (Ca²⁺ channel / ↓ACh release), improves with use and is paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why does an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor treat myasthenia gravis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It increases ACh in the cleft (pyridostigmine), giving more chance to bind the reduced receptors — but this is symptomatic relief only. Disease-modifying treatment is immunosuppression (corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent such as azathioprine) and thymectomy where indicated.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the mechanism and effect of botulinum toxin?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release presynaptically → flaccid paralysis (botulism); used therapeutically as botulinum toxin type A for targeted muscle relaxation.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the mechanism and effect of organophosphates?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: A cholinergic crisis — SLUDGE (salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, GI upset, emesis) plus bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, miosis, fasciculations and weakness; bronchorrhoea and bradycardia are what kill. Treat with decontamination (staff in protective equipment), then atropine titrated in escalating doses against secretions and chest signs, plus pralidoxime.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How do botulinum toxin and organophosphates contrast?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Botulinum ↓ACh (blocks release) → paralysis; organophosphates ↑↑ACh (block breakdown) → overstimulation → also paralysis (via depolarising block) — opposite mechanisms, both causing weakness.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is a depolarising muscle relaxant, and give an example?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Suxamethonium — it binds and ACTIVATES the receptor → sustained depolarisation → the muscle can't repolarise → initial fasciculation then flaccid paralysis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why is a depolarising blocker (suxamethonium) NOT reversed by anticholinesterases?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Because it causes sustained depolarisation; increasing ACh worsens the block. It wears off only as it is metabolised.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the cautions with suxamethonium?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It causes hyperkalaemia. The risk after a burn, crush injury or denervation is TIME-DEPENDENT: it is safe in the first 24 hours, then avoided from about 24-48 hours until healing is complete (months), because extrajunctional receptors upregulate. Also avoid in established hyperkalaemia, and where there is a personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia or of plasma cholinesterase deficiency (suxamethonium apnoea).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is a non-depolarising muscle relaxant, and give examples?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Rocuronium, vecuronium and atracurium — they competitively BLOCK (antagonise) the receptor → no depolarisation → paralysis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How are non-depolarising blockers reversed?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: By an anticholinesterase — neostigmine, always given with an antimuscarinic (glycopyrronium or atropine) to prevent bradycardia, bronchoconstriction and secretions — increasing ACh outcompetes the blocker; or by sugammadex, which binds rocuronium directly.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the key distinction between depolarising and non-depolarising relaxants?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Depolarising (suxamethonium) activates then blocks (fasciculations first, NOT reversed by neostigmine); non-depolarising competitively antagonises (reversed by neostigmine/sugammadex).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the difference between a myasthenic and a cholinergic crisis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Myasthenic crisis = too little ACh (weakness worsens, improves with edrophonium) — it is respiratory failure, needing urgent forced vital capacity monitoring (oxygen saturation is falsely reassuring), intensive care involvement and plasma exchange or IVIG. Cholinergic crisis = too much ACh (SLUDGE, fasciculations) — stop the anticholinesterase, give atropine for muscarinic features, and support ventilation. Many drugs precipitate myasthenic crisis: aminoglycosides, macrolides, quinolones, beta-blockers and magnesium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is bone, and what are its roles?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: A living, dynamic tissue constantly being remodelled — providing structural support, protecting organs, and acting as the body's calcium reservoir.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What keeps bone mass constant, and what controls it?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Bone mass stays constant while osteoblast and osteoclast activity are balanced; the balance is set by PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin (minor in humans), with oestrogen restraining osteoclasts.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the two components of bone matrix and their roles?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Organic (collagen, ~⅓) provides flexibility/tensile strength; mineral (hydroxyapatite = calcium + phosphate, ~⅔) provides hardness/compressive strength and the calcium store.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the two types of bone and their features?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Cortical (compact) bone — dense, the shaft, strength; and trabecular (cancellous/spongy) bone — metabolically active, the ends/vertebrae, where turnover and osteoporotic fractures happen.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the dual role of bone, and how can it conflict?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Bone is both structural AND a calcium reservoir — these can conflict, as the body will sacrifice bone to maintain blood calcium (via PTH).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What do osteoblasts do, and their origin?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: They build bone — laying down new matrix and mineralising it; they are of mesenchymal origin. (Memory hook: osteoBlasts Build.)

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What do osteoclasts do, and their origin?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: They break down (resorb) bone, releasing calcium and phosphate; they come from the monocyte/macrophage (haematopoietic) lineage. (Memory hook: osteoClasts Consume.)

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are osteocytes?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Mature osteoblasts trapped in bone that sense mechanical stress and regulate remodelling.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Describe the bone remodelling cycle.
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: A coupled cycle (~10% replaced per year): osteoclasts resorb old/damaged bone, then osteoblasts lay down new bone which is mineralised; resorption and formation are normally balanced, keeping bone mass constant.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why does bone remodel?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: To repair microdamage, adapt to mechanical load (Wolff's law), and release/store calcium for homeostasis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is Wolff's law?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress — so weight-bearing exercise builds bone.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What happens when the remodelling balance tips one way or the other?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Increased resorption (osteoclasts win) → bone loss → osteoporosis; reduced formation or mineralisation → weak bone → osteomalacia.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the effect of PTH on bone?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It acts on osteoblasts to increase RANKL, which increases osteoclast activity → bone resorption → releases calcium to raise blood Ca2+. Osteoclasts themselves have no PTH receptor — which is why anti-RANKL therapy (denosumab) works.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the effect of vitamin D (calcitriol) on bone?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It increases calcium absorption from the gut, supporting mineralisation; deficiency causes osteomalacia.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the effect of oestrogen on bone, and its clinical relevance?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Oestrogen restrains osteoclasts, protecting bone; its loss at menopause causes unrestrained resorption → postmenopausal osteoporosis (the commonest cause).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the calcium-vs-bone conflict with chronically high PTH?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: PTH raises blood calcium partly by resorbing bone, so chronically high PTH (hyperparathyroidism, CKD) causes bone loss — the body sacrifices the skeleton to maintain blood calcium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What defines osteoporosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Reduced bone MASS (resorption > formation) with NORMAL mineralisation → brittle, fragile bone → fragility fractures (hip, vertebrae, wrist); causes include postmenopausal oestrogen loss, age and steroids.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What defines osteomalacia/rickets?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Reduced MINERALISATION (soft bone) due to vitamin D deficiency → soft, bendy bone with pain and fractures (bowed legs in children with rickets).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How do osteoporosis and osteomalacia differ?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Osteoporosis = too little bone (normal mineralisation); osteomalacia = poorly mineralised bone (soft, vitamin D deficiency) — different problems, different treatment.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What defines Paget's disease of bone?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Disordered, excessive (chaotic) remodelling → enlarged, weak, deformed bone with markedly raised ALP and bone pain.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is CKD bone disease (renal osteodystrophy)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Reduced vitamin D activation (↓1-α-hydroxylation) + phosphate retention → secondary hyperparathyroidism → increased bone resorption.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How do bisphosphonates work, and their uses?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts → reduced resorption. Oral alendronate is first-line for osteoporosis; also used in Paget's. For hypercalcaemia the treatment is an INTRAVENOUS bisphosphonate after intravenous rehydration — not oral alendronate. Correct calcium and vitamin D first; take on an empty stomach with plain water and stay upright for 30 minutes; counsel about new thigh or groin pain (atypical femoral fracture) and dental review (osteonecrosis of the jaw) (MHRA).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How do denosumab and teriparatide work?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL → reduces osteoclast formation. It must NOT be stopped or a dose delayed without specialist advice — rebound bone turnover on stopping causes multiple vertebral fractures; correct and supplement calcium and vitamin D.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why is ALP a marker of bone turnover?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: ALP rises in states of high bone turnover — Paget's disease, osteomalacia and bone metastases.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the three distinct MSK roles of calcium?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: (1) Intracellular calcium triggers muscle contraction; (2) extracellular/blood calcium sets neuromuscular excitability; (3) bone calcium provides structure and acts as the body's reservoir.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How do the intracellular and extracellular calcium pools differ?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Intracellular calcium (the contraction trigger, released from the SR) is a SEPARATE pool from extracellular/blood calcium (which sets excitability); blood calcium disorders affect excitability, not the contraction machinery directly.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Where does the calcium that triggers skeletal muscle contraction come from?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) — this intracellular pool is tightly controlled and separate from blood calcium (in cardiac muscle, extracellular calcium also contributes via calcium-induced calcium release).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How does calcium trigger contraction in skeletal muscle?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It is the 'on-switch' — AP → T-tubules → SR releases calcium → calcium binds troponin → moves tropomyosin → exposes actin sites → cross-bridge cycle → contraction; relaxation pumps calcium back into the SR (active, uses ATP).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What does extracellular (blood) calcium do to nerve and muscle membranes?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It sets their excitability — calcium sits on the membrane and stabilises it, raising the threshold for firing (making it harder to depolarise).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the counterintuitive effect of LOW blood calcium (hypocalcaemia)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Low ionised calcium destabilises the resting membrane potential, making nerves and muscle MORE excitable — tetany, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, and in severe cases laryngospasm and seizures, with a prolonged QT and arrhythmia risk. Acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia needs intravenous calcium gluconate with continuous ECG monitoring; check and correct magnesium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What is the effect of HIGH blood calcium (hypercalcaemia) on excitability?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: High calcium stabilises the membrane, making nerves and muscle LESS excitable — weakness, lethargy, hyporeflexia, constipation and confusion. Management is intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride rehydration first, then an intravenous bisphosphonate.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why is the effect of blood calcium on excitability counterintuitive?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Because calcium STABILISES the membrane (it is not directly doing the firing) — so low calcium → MORE excitable (tetany) and high calcium → LESS excitable (weakness), the opposite of what students expect.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why does alkalosis (e.g. hyperventilation) cause tetany despite normal total calcium?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: It is the ionised (free) calcium that matters — alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin → ↓ionised calcium → tetany (perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm) despite a normal total calcium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why must total calcium be corrected for albumin?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Because it is the ionised fraction that is physiologically active — low albumin gives a low total calcium but a normal ionised calcium, so total calcium is corrected for albumin.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How much of the body's calcium is in bone, and in what form?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: About 99%, stored as hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: What are the two (potentially conflicting) roles of calcium in bone?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Structural — hydroxyapatite gives bone its hardness/compressive strength; and reservoir — bone is the body's calcium bank, releasing (resorption) or storing (formation) calcium to maintain blood calcium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why does chronically high PTH cause bone loss?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Maintaining blood calcium takes priority over the skeleton — when blood calcium falls, PTH resorbs bone to release calcium, so chronically high PTH (hyperparathyroidism, CKD) causes bone loss (the body sacrifices bone to defend blood calcium).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: How is blood calcium kept constant?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: PTH (raises calcium: resorbs bone, increases renal reabsorption, activates vitamin D) and vitamin D (increases gut calcium absorption) — keeping blood calcium in the tight range needed for normal neuromuscular excitability.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.front: Why does tetany occur after a thyroidectomy?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.back: Inadvertent parathyroid damage → hypocalcaemia → increased neuromuscular excitability → tetany.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: What three tests should synovial fluid from a joint aspiration be sent for?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Polarised light microscopy (crystals), Gram stain + culture (infection), and cell count/WCC. Never send microscopy alone.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Describe gout (MSU) crystals under polarised light microscopy.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Monosodium urate: needle-shaped and negatively birefringent — appear yellow when parallel to the red compensator axis (blue when perpendicular). Mnemonic: needles, negative, yellow-parallel.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Describe pseudogout (CPPD) crystals under polarised light microscopy.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate: rhomboid/brick-shaped and positively birefringent — appear blue when parallel to the compensator axis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Does a crystal-positive aspirate exclude septic arthritis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: No. Crystals and infection can coexist. A hot, swollen joint must be treated as septic until proven otherwise — always send Gram stain, culture and cell count, and aspirate before starting antibiotics.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Give the classic joint and key associations for gout vs pseudogout.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Gout: first MTP joint (podagra); high urate, alcohol, diuretics, renal impairment. Pseudogout/CPPD: knee/wrist with chondrocalcinosis on X-ray; older age, haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: What is the single most important diagnostic step in a suspected hot septic joint, and what is its timing relative to antibiotics?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Urgent joint aspiration (arthrocentesis) — must be performed BEFORE starting antibiotics. Send fluid for cell count/differential, Gram stain, culture & sensitivities and polarised microscopy for crystals. In a septic/unwell patient take blood cultures and do not delay IV antibiotics once the joint has been sampled.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Give the approximate synovial fluid white cell count (WCC) bands: normal, non-inflammatory (OA), inflammatory (RA/gout), septic.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Normal <200 (clear, viscous); non-inflammatory/OA <2,000; inflammatory/RA/gout ~2,000–50,000; septic usually >50,000 (often >100,000) with >75% neutrophils, turbid/purulent, low viscosity. No cut-off is absolute — treat on clinical suspicion.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: How sensitive is the synovial fluid Gram stain in septic arthritis, and what does a negative result mean?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Only ~50% sensitive — a NEGATIVE Gram stain does NOT exclude septic arthritis. Culture is more sensitive but slower. Also remember the presence of crystals does not exclude coexistent infection.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Name the commonest causative organism of septic arthritis and two organisms suggested by specific patient groups.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Commonest = Staphylococcus aureus. Consider Neisseria gonorrhoeae in young sexually active adults; Gram-negative organisms in the elderly, IV drug users and immunocompromised.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: What are the four Kocher criteria used to distinguish septic arthritis of the hip from transient synovitis in children?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, raised ESR, and raised WCC. The more criteria present, the higher the probability of septic arthritis — a higher score warrants aspiration/surgical management.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: What do the mnemonics OA = LOSS and RA = LESS stand for on X-ray?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: OA = LOSS: Loss of joint space (asymmetrical), Osteophytes, Subchondral Sclerosis, Subchondral cysts. RA = LESS: Loss of joint space (symmetrical), Erosions, Soft-tissue swelling, Soft bones (periarticular osteopenia).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: How does joint distribution distinguish RA from OA in the hand?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: RA: symmetrical, affects MCP, PIP and wrist joints and SPARES the DIPs. OA: affects DIP (Heberden's nodes), PIP (Bouchard's nodes), 1st carpometacarpal (thumb base 'squaring') and weight-bearing joints (hip, knee, spine).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Why is a mnemonic like 'bone-forming vs bone-destroying' useful for OA vs RA?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: OA is degenerative and bone-FORMING — it produces osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis. RA is inflammatory and bone-DESTROYING — it produces marginal erosions and periarticular osteopenia. Both share loss of joint space, but the productive vs erosive pattern separates them.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Does a normal hand X-ray exclude rheumatoid arthritis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: No. Radiographic erosions and osteopenia are late findings; early RA films may show only soft-tissue swelling or be completely normal. Ultrasound and MRI detect early synovitis/erosions, and diagnosis rests on clinical features plus RF/anti-CCP and ESR/CRP. Refer for early inflammatory arthritis assessment (window of opportunity for DMARDs).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Name the classic late hand deformities of rheumatoid arthritis.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Ulnar deviation of the fingers at the MCP joints, swan-neck deformity, boutonnière deformity and Z-thumb. These reflect long-standing erosive/inflammatory joint and tendon damage.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Why can USS and MRI diagnose RA earlier than plain X-ray?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: They visualise soft-tissue synovial inflammation (synovitis) and early erosions/bone oedema, which precede the bony erosions and joint space narrowing seen on X-ray. X-ray is often normal in early RA, so relying on it delays diagnosis until damage is irreversible.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: What does power Doppler signal on ultrasound indicate in RA?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Increased synovial vascularity, marking ACTIVE inflammation. Power Doppler signal correlates with disease activity and helps distinguish active synovitis from inactive synovial thickening; it is used to assess activity and treatment response.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for early RA, and what unique prognostic finding does it show?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: MRI. It detects synovitis (with gadolinium enhancement), erosions not yet seen on X-ray, and crucially BONE MARROW OEDEMA (osteitis) — a pre-erosive change that predicts future erosions and is prognostic.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: A patient has inflammatory polyarthritis but a normal X-ray. What should you conclude and do?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: A normal X-ray does NOT exclude active RA. Use USS (power Doppler) or MRI to detect early/subclinical synovitis, and refer promptly to rheumatology for DMARDs within the 'window of opportunity' before irreversible damage.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: List the main clinical uses of USS/MRI in rheumatoid arthritis.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Confirming synovitis in early/equivocal inflammatory arthritis; detecting subclinical synovitis; assessing disease activity and treatment response (power Doppler); and detecting erosions and bone marrow oedema for prognosis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: What is the earliest MRI finding of active sacroiliitis in axial spondyloarthritis, and on which sequence?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Subchondral bone marrow oedema (osteitis) adjacent to the SI joints, seen as high signal on STIR / T2 fat-saturated sequences. It is the key ASAS active lesion and appears before any X-ray change.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Why request MRI rather than plain X-ray in a young patient with inflammatory back pain?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Plain films only show established (late) sacroiliitis and are insensitive early. MRI detects active inflammation (bone marrow oedema) before structural damage, allowing early diagnosis and DMARD/biologic therapy. A normal X-ray does NOT exclude axial SpA.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: List the classic late plain-film spinal signs of ankylosing spondylitis.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Bamboo spine (vertical marginal syndesmophytes bridging vertebrae + ligament ossification), squaring of vertebral bodies (from Romanus lesions / shiny corners), and the dagger sign (central ossified interspinous/supraspinous ligament on AP film).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: How is radiographic sacroiliitis graded and what does the modified New York criterion require?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Graded 0–4 (0 normal, 1 suspicious, 2 minimal erosions/sclerosis, 3 definite erosions+sclerosis+widening/narrowing, 4 total ankylosis). Modified New York requires grade >=2 bilaterally OR grade 3–4 unilaterally.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Why is new back pain after minor trauma a red flag in an ankylosing spondylitis patient?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: The fused, rigid bamboo spine is brittle and fractures easily, often as an unstable transverse fracture through the ankylosed segment, risking spinal cord injury. Plain films often miss these — have a low threshold for CT/MRI.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: How do RF and anti-CCP differ in suspected rheumatoid arthritis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: RF is sensitive but non-specific (positive in Sjögren’s, SLE, hepatitis C, healthy elderly). Anti-CCP is highly specific (~95%) and predicts erosive/aggressive disease. ~30% of RA is seronegative — negative serology does not exclude RA; refer on clinical grounds within the window of opportunity.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.front: Outline the management sequence once urate crystals confirm gout.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.back: Acute attack: NSAID, colchicine or a short steroid course. Urate-lowering (allopurinol) is started LATER (not during the attack) with NSAID/colchicine cover. Recheck serum urate 4–6 weeks after the flare settles (it can be normal during an acute attack).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: What does a DEXA T-score compare BMD against, and what are the WHO diagnostic thresholds?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: T-score = SD from the mean BMD of a YOUNG healthy adult (same sex). WHO: ≥ −1.0 = normal; −1.0 to −2.5 = osteopenia; ≤ −2.5 = osteoporosis; ≤ −2.5 plus a fragility fracture = severe/established osteoporosis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: When do you use the Z-score instead of the T-score, and what does a low Z-score imply?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Use the Z-score (age-matched reference) in younger patients, premenopausal women and children. A low Z-score is unexpectedly low for age and should trigger a search for a secondary cause of bone loss (e.g. steroids, coeliac, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, myeloma, hypogonadism).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: What does FRAX calculate and what is it used for?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: FRAX estimates the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture and of hip fracture, using clinical risk factors (age, sex, BMI, previous fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, alcohol, steroids, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis) with or without femoral neck BMD. The result is mapped (NOGG) to reassure, measure BMD/DEXA, or treat.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: What is a fragility fracture and why does it matter for osteoporosis diagnosis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: A fracture caused by low-energy trauma — a fall from standing height or less. It indicates osteoporosis regardless of BMD and warrants treatment even if the DEXA T-score is not in the osteoporotic range.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: Which two skeletal sites are standardly scanned by DEXA and why?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: The lumbar spine (L1–L4) and the hip (femoral neck) — the clinically important fracture sites. DEXA is the gold-standard, low-radiation test for diagnosing osteoporosis and assessing fracture risk.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: What is the underlying bone abnormality in osteomalacia, and what is its childhood equivalent?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Osteomalacia = defective mineralisation of osteoid in the adult skeleton. The childhood equivalent, occurring before growth-plate fusion, is rickets. Both are most commonly due to vitamin D deficiency.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: Describe Looser's zones and their characteristic sites.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Looser's zones (pseudofractures / Milkman lines) are narrow lucent bands of unmineralised osteoid running perpendicular to the cortex, often bilateral and symmetrical. Classic sites: medial femoral neck, pubic rami, lateral border of scapula, and ribs.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: Give the classic biochemistry panel of osteomalacia.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Low vitamin D (25-OH), low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: How does the biochemistry of osteomalacia differ from osteoporosis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: In osteomalacia the biochemistry is abnormal (low vit D, low/normal Ca, low PO4, high ALP, high PTH). In osteoporosis routine bone biochemistry (Ca, PO4, ALP, PTH) is normal.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: What are the plain-film features of rickets in a child?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Cupping, fraying and widening of the metaphyses (best at wrists/knees), a widened growth plate, and bowing of long bones (genu varum). Costochondral swelling gives the rachitic rosary.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: Which periosteal reactions are classic for osteosarcoma, and where does osteosarcoma typically arise?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Codman triangle (ossified edge of lifted periosteum) and sunburst/sun-ray spiculation. Osteosarcoma affects adolescents/young adults, in the metaphysis around the knee (distal femur, proximal tibia).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: An onion-skin (lamellated, multi-layered) periosteal reaction in the diaphysis of a child suggests which tumour?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Ewing sarcoma — children/young people, diaphysis of long bones or pelvis, often with a soft-tissue mass and systemic features that can mimic osteomyelitis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: List the X-ray features that favour an aggressive/malignant bone lesion.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Wide zone of transition (ill-defined margin), permeative/moth-eaten destruction, cortical destruction/breach, associated soft-tissue mass, and aggressive periosteal reaction (Codman/sunburst/onion-skin).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: What is the correct work-up sequence for a suspected primary bone tumour?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Plain X-ray first, then MRI for local staging, CT chest plus bone scan/PET for distant staging, and referral to a specialist sarcoma MDT/centre where biopsy is performed.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: Why must biopsy of a suspected bone sarcoma be done at the specialist centre?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: A poorly planned biopsy tract contaminates tissue compartments and can compromise limb-salvage surgery, potentially converting a salvageable limb into an amputation.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: In an older adult with a destructive bone lesion, which malignancies are most likely?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Metastases and myeloma are the commonest malignant bone lesions overall; chondrosarcoma also favours older adults.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: Give the Ca/PO₄/ALP/PTH pattern for osteoporosis, osteomalacia, primary hyperPTH, Paget’s and CKD-MBD.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Osteoporosis: all normal. Osteomalacia: ↓vitD, ↓/N Ca, ↓PO₄, ↑ALP, ↑PTH. Primary hyperPTH: ↑Ca, ↓PO₄, ↑PTH. Paget’s: isolated ↑ALP. CKD-MBD: ↑PO₄, ↓Ca, ↑PTH, ↑ALP. Use albumin-corrected calcium.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: An isolated raised ALP with normal Ca, PO₄ and PTH — diagnosis and next steps?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Paget’s disease. Confirm with X-ray + isotope bone scan; treat symptomatic disease with a bisphosphonate. Watch for deafness, high-output cardiac failure, pathological fracture and rare osteosarcoma.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.front: How is an oral bisphosphonate taken and what are its key adverse effects?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.back: Take on an empty stomach with water and remain upright ~30 min. Key adverse effects: oesophagitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fractures. Alternatives: denosumab, teriparatide, IV zoledronate.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: What is the central clinical role of nailfold capillaroscopy?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: To distinguish PRIMARY from SECONDARY Raynaud's phenomenon and to detect early systemic sclerosis (SSc) — often before other clinical features appear. A normal study supports benign primary Raynaud's; a scleroderma pattern indicates an underlying/evolving connective tissue disease.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: Name the four components of the "scleroderma pattern" on capillaroscopy.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: 1) Giant (dilated) capillaries, 2) Microhaemorrhages, 3) Capillary loss / avascular areas (dropout), 4) Architectural disorganisation and branching loops.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: How do primary and secondary Raynaud's differ on capillaroscopy and serology?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: Primary: younger, symmetrical, no tissue damage, NORMAL capillaroscopy, negative autoantibodies — benign. Secondary: scleroderma-pattern capillaroscopy plus positive autoantibodies (ANA, anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70) — points to SSc/CTD.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: Which autoantibodies map to which systemic sclerosis subtype?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: Anti-centromere antibody → limited cutaneous SSc / CREST. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) → diffuse cutaneous SSc.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: Why is capillaroscopy considered high-yield beyond bedside diagnosis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: It is part of the ACR/EULAR classification criteria for systemic sclerosis and predicts progression from isolated Raynaud's to definite SSc, especially when combined with an SSc-specific antibody.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: What is the characteristic temporal artery ultrasound finding in giant cell arteritis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: The halo sign — a hypoechoic, circumferential wall thickening (mural oedema) around the artery lumen. A non-compressible artery (positive compression sign) also indicates vasculitis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: List the classic temporal artery biopsy histology findings in GCA.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: Transmural granulomatous inflammation, multinucleate giant cells, intimal thickening, and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: Why does a negative temporal artery biopsy NOT exclude GCA?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: The inflammation is patchy with skip lesions, so a biopsy segment can miss affected areas. Take an adequate length (~1–2 cm) and multiple sections; GCA remains a clinical diagnosis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: Should you delay starting steroids to wait for the temporal artery biopsy in suspected GCA?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: No. Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately on clinical suspicion. The biopsy remains positive for ~1–2 weeks after starting steroids, so treat first and confirm later.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: How does management differ when a patient with suspected GCA has visual symptoms?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: Visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax, sudden visual loss, diplopia) signal impending irreversible blindness — give IV methylprednisolone immediately, rather than oral prednisolone, as an emergency.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: How is ANA used in suspected SLE, and what does a negative result mean?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: ANA is a sensitive but non-specific screen; a negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely. A positive ANA reflexes to specific antibodies (anti-dsDNA + ENA panel); low-titre positives are common and non-specific.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: What do a rising anti-dsDNA and falling C3/C4 indicate, and what do you do?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: Active SLE / lupus nephritis (anti-dsDNA is specific and tracks activity; low complement = consumption). Check urine protein:creatinine ratio + urinalysis for red-cell casts and refer for renal assessment ± biopsy.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: Map the ENA antibodies to their diseases.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: Anti-Sm → SLE (specific). Anti-Ro/La → Sjögren’s (+ neonatal lupus/congenital heart block). Anti-U1-RNP → mixed CTD. Anti-Jo-1 → poly/dermatomyositis. Anti-centromere → limited SSc/CREST. Anti-Scl-70 → diffuse SSc.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: How do the ANCA subtypes map, and what is the urgent work-up?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: c-ANCA/PR3 → GPA; p-ANCA/MPO → microscopic polyangiitis & eosinophilic GPA. Same-day: urinalysis (red-cell casts), U&E/creatinine, CXR for pulmonary–renal syndrome; treat with steroids + cyclophosphamide/rituximab.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.front: What organ surveillance do the systemic sclerosis antibodies trigger?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.back: Anti-centromere (limited/CREST) → annual echo + PFT for pulmonary hypertension. Anti-Scl-70 (diffuse) → HRCT + PFT (DLCO) for ILD, and BP monitoring for scleroderma renal crisis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: How should you describe a fracture on X-ray systematically?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Two orthogonal views (AP + lateral) plus the joint above and below. Then: which bone and where (proximal/mid/distal third), open vs closed, pattern (transverse/oblique/spiral/comminuted/segmental; greenstick/buckle in children), displacement, angulation, rotation, shortening, and whether it is intra-articular.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Garden classification: which grades are displaced and what is the management implication?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Garden I = incomplete/valgus impacted, II = complete undisplaced (I–II are undisplaced → often internal fixation). III = partially displaced, IV = fully displaced (III–IV are displaced → disrupt retrograde blood supply → high AVN risk → arthroplasty, hemi or THR). "1 & 2 fix, 3 & 4 replace."

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Weber classification of ankle fractures and its significance?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Level of the lateral malleolus/fibular fracture relative to the syndesmosis: A = below (syndesmosis intact, usually stable), B = at the level (variable stability), C = above (syndesmosis disrupted, unstable, usually needs ORIF). Higher = more unstable. A high fibular fracture with medial injury = Maisonneuve.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Salter-Harris classification (SALTR mnemonic) and prognosis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: I Slipped (through physis), II Above (into metaphysis — commonest), III beLow (into epiphysis, intra-articular), IV Through/Transverse (metaphysis + physis + epiphysis), V cRush (compression of physis, worst prognosis). Higher grades → higher risk of growth arrest. Types I and V may look radiographically normal.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Which fracture scenarios are surgical emergencies requiring immediate referral?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Open fractures, fractures with neurovascular compromise, and compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch). Manage open fractures with analgesia, photograph, saline-gauze cover, splint, tetanus cover, IV antibiotics, and urgent orthopaedic referral — don't delay for classification.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What is the commonest carpal bone fracture and its classic mechanism?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: The scaphoid — most commonly fractured after a fall on the outstretched hand (FOOSH).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Does a normal initial X-ray exclude a scaphoid fracture?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: No. Early plain films are frequently normal despite a real (occult) fracture. Snuffbox tenderness with a normal X-ray must be immobilised and re-imaged — MRI (most sensitive) or repeat radiographs at 10–14 days. Do not discharge.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What are 'scaphoid views' and why is the PA in ulnar deviation important?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: A dedicated series of ~4 wrist radiographs. The PA in ulnar deviation elongates and profiles the scaphoid, making a waist fracture line more visible than on standard views.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Why do proximal pole scaphoid fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply entering distally (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery), so the proximal pole is perfused last — proximal fractures risk AVN and non-union.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: How do you manage a suspected occult scaphoid fracture (snuffbox tenderness + normal X-ray)?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Immobilise in a scaphoid/thumb-spica cast and either repeat radiographs at ~10–14 days or obtain MRI (most sensitive, increasingly first-line) or CT. Never simply reassure and discharge.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: On a lateral elbow radiograph, when is a POSTERIOR fat pad significant?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: ALWAYS abnormal. The posterior fat pad is normally hidden deep in the olecranon fossa, so ANY visible posterior fat pad indicates a joint effusion/haemarthrosis — i.e. an occult intra-articular fracture until proven otherwise.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What is the "sail sign"?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: An elevated ANTERIOR fat pad lifted off the distal humerus by a joint effusion, producing a triangular lucency resembling a billowing sail. It indicates a haemarthrosis and therefore a likely intra-articular fracture.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: A fat pad sign with no visible fracture line — what is the likely occult fracture in an ADULT vs a CHILD?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Adult: radial head fracture (commonest). Child: supracondylar fracture (also lateral condyle). Manage as an occult fracture: immobilise and arrange orthopaedic follow-up with repeat imaging.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What does the CRITOE mnemonic describe, and what are the approximate ages?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Order of appearance of paediatric elbow ossification centres: Capitellum ~1, Radial head ~3, Internal (medial) epicondyle ~5, Trochlea ~7, Olecranon ~9, External (lateral) epicondyle ~11. Used to avoid mistaking a normal centre for a fracture (or vice versa).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Which structures are at risk in a displaced paediatric supracondylar fracture, and what must be assessed?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: The brachial artery and the median/anterior interosseous (AIN) and radial nerves. Check distal pulse, capillary refill and the 'OK' sign (AIN). Urgent referral if displaced or neurovascular compromise — risk of Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: An elderly patient falls, has groin pain and cannot weight-bear, but the hip X-ray is normal. What must you consider?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: An occult neck-of-femur (NOF) fracture. Around 2–10% of NOF fractures are invisible on the initial plain film — a normal X-ray does NOT exclude a hip fracture.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: If a hip fracture is clinically suspected but not seen on X-ray, what is the investigation of choice?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: MRI — the most sensitive test. It detects the fracture line and bone-marrow oedema within hours of injury, before any radiographic change appears. (NICE/BOAST guidance.)

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: When is CT used instead of MRI for a suspected occult hip fracture?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: When MRI is unavailable or contraindicated within 24 hours. CT is the second-line alternative but can miss non-displaced or impacted fractures because it relies on visible cortical/trabecular disruption rather than marrow signal.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Which clinical signs suggest an occult hip fracture even with a normal X-ray?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Inability to weight-bear, groin pain, pain on axial loading/log-roll, and inability to straight-leg raise. Classic shortening and external rotation may be ABSENT if the fracture is undisplaced or impacted.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Why is it dangerous to miss an occult hip fracture and let the patient mobilise?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Weight-bearing can displace it, converting a fixable fracture into a displaced intracapsular fracture with much higher risk of avascular necrosis (AVN) and non-union, plus the high morbidity/mortality of delayed hip-fracture surgery.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: In suspected femoral-head AVN, why is a normal plain X-ray insufficient to exclude the diagnosis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Plain radiographs are normal in early AVN. MRI is the earliest and most sensitive test — it detects marrow oedema and the double-line sign (Ficat I) before any radiographic change, so a normal X-ray never rules out AVN.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What is the 'double-line sign' and where is it seen?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: An MRI finding (best on T2) of femoral-head AVN: a low-signal outer sclerotic rim with a high-signal inner line at the reactive necrotic/viable interface. It is essentially pathognomonic (though marrow oedema is the earliest MRI change).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What does the 'crescent sign' on X-ray represent and which Ficat stage is it?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: A subchondral lucent crescent paralleling the articular surface, representing subchondral fracture/collapse of the femoral head. It corresponds to Ficat stage III.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Outline Ficat staging 0–IV of AVN.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: 0 = X-ray and MRI normal; I = X-ray normal, MRI positive; II = sclerosis/cysts, no collapse; III = crescent sign / subchondral collapse with head flattening; IV = joint-space narrowing and secondary osteoarthritis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: How does management of femoral-head AVN differ pre- vs post-collapse?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Pre-collapse (Ficat I–II): joint-preserving measures — core decompression, bisphosphonates, treat the cause. Post-collapse (Ficat III–IV): total hip arthroplasty. Early MRI diagnosis is what enables joint preservation.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What two safety steps must bracket every fracture/dislocation reduction or manipulation?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: (1) Document distal neurovascular status BOTH before and after the procedure, and (2) obtain a post-reduction / check X-ray (two views) to confirm relocation/adequate alignment and cast or hardware position. Image again after cast application.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Anterior shoulder dislocation — which nerve is at risk and how do you test it?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: The axillary nerve. Test sensation over the 'regimental badge' area of the lateral deltoid and deltoid motor function (contraction) — do not rely on painful abduction post-reduction. Document pre- and post-reduction.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Why is a knee dislocation a surgical emergency even when foot pulses are palpable?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: It is a popliteal artery injury until proven otherwise — an intimal tear can thrombose later despite initially palpable pulses. Assess pulses/ABPI and have a low threshold for CT angiography even if pulses are present.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Nerve-at-risk pairings to memorise for reductions/fractures.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Shoulder dislocation → axillary nerve; humeral shaft fracture → radial nerve (wrist drop); supracondylar/elbow → brachial artery + median/anterior interosseous ± radial; posterior hip dislocation → sciatic nerve; knee dislocation → popliteal artery.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: A patient develops absent radial pulse and new median nerve signs immediately after supracondylar reduction. Action?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: This is an emergency. Re-assess neurovascular status, gently re-position/reduce and release any tight cast/flexion, and obtain urgent senior orthopaedic ± vascular review; the pink pulseless hand may need surgical exploration. Also watch for compartment syndrome.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What are the earliest and most sensitive clinical signs of acute compartment syndrome?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the compartment muscles. Paraesthesia follows. Pulselessness and paralysis are LATE signs — do not wait for them.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Why is 'pulselessness' a dangerous sign to rely on in compartment syndrome?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: It is a late sign — the limb can be irreversibly damaged (muscle/nerve necrosis) while distal pulses are still palpable. Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis; act on pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What intracompartmental pressure thresholds indicate the need for fasciotomy?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: An absolute compartment pressure >30–40 mmHg, OR — more reliably — a delta pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) of <30 mmHg. Measurement is reserved for equivocal or obtunded/unconscious patients.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: How should a limb with suspected compartment syndrome be positioned, and what is the definitive treatment?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Keep the limb at heart level (NOT elevated above the heart, which reduces perfusion); split all circumferential casts/dressings to skin; give oxygen and analgesia. Definitive treatment is urgent open fasciotomy decompressing all compartments.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: What are the commonest cause and the main complications of untreated acute compartment syndrome?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Commonest cause: tibial (and forearm) fractures. Complications of delay: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture, rhabdomyolysis with AKI, and amputation/limb loss.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Which fracture patterns should raise suspicion of non-accidental injury, and what do you do?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: Metaphyseal corner/bucket-handle, posterior rib fractures, multiple fractures of differing ages, or any fracture in a non-ambulant infant, plus a delayed/inconsistent history. Action: senior/paediatric input, skeletal survey, document, urgent safeguarding referral — do not discharge.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.front: Why is a long-bone fracture in a non-ambulant infant a red flag?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.back: A child who cannot yet walk or cruise should not sustain a long-bone (e.g. spiral femoral) fracture from normal handling; it implies applied force and mandates a safeguarding assessment and skeletal survey.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: Why is ultrasound preferred over MRI for superficial soft-tissue MSK problems?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: USS is cheap, radiation-free, real-time and dynamic (image during movement), allows side-to-side comparison, and guides injections/aspirations. It is ideal for superficial tendons, muscles, bursae and fluid collections. (MRI is better for deep structures, bone and marrow.)

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: What are the USS findings of a complete Achilles tendon rupture?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: A hypo-/anechoic gap between retracted, frayed tendon ends, with the gap changing on dynamic ankle movement. USS complements the clinical Simmonds'/Thompson calf-squeeze test.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: Which rotator cuff tendon is most commonly assessed on shoulder USS, and what can be seen?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: Supraspinatus. USS detects partial- and full-thickness tears, tendinopathy, calcific tendinitis, and subacromial-subdeltoid bursitis; dynamic scanning can show subacromial impingement during abduction.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: Where does a Baker's cyst arise and why is a ruptured one clinically important?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: It is a fluid collection in the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa of the popliteal fossa, often communicating with the knee joint. A ruptured Baker's cyst causes acute calf pain/swelling that mimics a DVT ('pseudothrombophlebitis'), so DVT must be excluded.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: List MSK ultrasound uses beyond tendon pathology.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: Joint effusions, ganglia, radiolucent foreign bodies, muscle tears/haematoma, and USS-guided joint/bursal injection or aspiration.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: What is the most sensitive and specific imaging test for osteomyelitis, and its key early sign?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: MRI. The hallmark early finding is bone marrow oedema: low signal on T1 and high signal on T2 / STIR (fat-suppressed). MRI is especially superior in early disease, the diabetic foot, and the spine.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: Why can a normal plain X-ray not exclude osteomyelitis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: X-ray is insensitive early — changes lag by ~10–14 days. The late findings are periosteal reaction, lytic destruction, sequestrum (dead necrotic bone), and involucrum (new periosteal bone around it). MRI shows disease long before these appear.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: Define sequestrum and involucrum in chronic osteomyelitis.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: Sequestrum = a fragment of dead, necrotic bone separated from viable bone. Involucrum = a sheath of new periosteal bone that forms around the sequestrum. Both are late X-ray signs.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for identifying the causative organism in osteomyelitis, and which organisms should you consider?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: Bone biopsy / culture — it guides targeted antibiotics. Commonest organism is Staphylococcus aureus; Salmonella in sickle-cell disease; consider TB and Pseudomonas (IVDU). Blood cultures and CRP/ESR support the diagnosis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: Which two osteomyelitis contexts are the classic must-not-miss red flags?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: (1) A diabetic foot ulcer that probes to bone / is non-healing — suspect osteomyelitis, get MRI. (2) Vertebral osteomyelitis (back pain + fever + raised markers) with risk of an epidural abscess — new neurology is a surgical emergency needing urgent whole-spine MRI.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: What do the letters GALS stand for, and what type of examination is it?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: Gait, Arms, Legs, Spine. It is a rapid locomotor SCREENING examination to detect significant musculoskeletal disease in a patient without an obvious regional complaint — a screen, not a diagnosis. Positive findings direct you to a focused regional exam (REMS).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: What are the three GALS screening questions?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: (1) Any pain or stiffness in your muscles, joints or back? (2) Any difficulty dressing yourself? (3) Any difficulty going up or down stairs? Normal answers make significant MSK disease unlikely.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: Describe the modified Schober's test technique.
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: Patient standing. Mark the midline at the posterior superior iliac spines (dimples of Venus, ~L5/lumbosacral junction), then mark 10 cm above and 5 cm below (15 cm span). Patient flexes forward maximally and the top-to-bottom distance is re-measured.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: What modified Schober's result indicates reduced lumbar flexion, and what condition does it suggest?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: An increase of LESS THAN 5 cm on forward flexion (i.e. the 15 cm span fails to reach 20 cm) indicates reduced lumbar flexion — classically seen in ankylosing spondylitis / axial spondyloarthritis. A normal test increases by more than 5 cm.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: A 28-year-old with inflammatory back pain has a reduced Schober's test. What is the next-step work-up?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: Axial spondyloarthritis work-up: MRI of the sacroiliac joints (for sacroiliitis / bone-marrow oedema) and HLA-B27 testing, alongside inflammatory markers and screening for extra-articular features (uveitis, psoriasis, IBD, enthesitis, dactylitis).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: What USS findings indicate active synovitis, and what do you do next?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: Grey-scale synovial hypertrophy plus power Doppler signal = active synovitis; USS also detects erosions earlier than plain film. This routes the patient into the inflammatory arthritis pathway (serology/DMARD decisions).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.front: What imaging is used for osteomyelitis if MRI is contraindicated?
