investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.back: A radionuclide bone scan or a labelled-white-cell scan as second-line (e.g. when metalwork or a pacemaker precludes MRI). MRI remains first-line where possible; bone biopsy/culture is the gold standard for the organism.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: How are the vasculitides principally classified?
options: By the SIZE of vessel predominantly affected (large/medium/small)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: By the SIZE of vessel predominantly affected (large/medium/small)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Vasculitides are classified by vessel size, which predicts the presentation (e.g. large-vessel → cranial ischaemia; small-vessel ANCA → pulmonary–renal).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which vasculitis presents in the over-50s with temporal headache, jaw claudication and visual loss with a raised ESR?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Giant cell arteritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Giant cell arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis of the elderly with temporal headache, jaw claudication and sight-threatening visual loss.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with a small-vessel vasculitis has a saddle-nose deformity, sinusitis, lung involvement and glomerulonephritis, with positive cANCA/PR3. Which condition is this?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: ENT (saddle nose/sinusitis) + lung + kidney involvement with cANCA/PR3 is granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient has recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and a positive pathergy test. Which vasculitis is this?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Behçet's disease
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Recurrent oral + genital ulcers with uveitis and pathergy is Behçet's disease (a variable-vessel vasculitis).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: In a patient with suspected ANCA-associated vasculitis, which bedside/simple investigations are essential?
options: Renal function and a urine dip (for a pulmonary–renal syndrome)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Renal function and a urine dip (for a pulmonary–renal syndrome)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Renal function and urine dip are essential to detect the pulmonary–renal syndrome of ANCA-associated vasculitis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A 72-year-old woman has a new right-sided headache, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, and jaw pain when chewing. Her right temporal artery is tender and thickened. What is the diagnosis and immediate action?
options: Giant cell arteritis; start high-dose steroids immediately (before biopsy)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Giant cell arteritis; start high-dose steroids immediately (before biopsy)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: New headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and a tender temporal artery in an elderly patient is GCA — start high-dose steroids at once without waiting for the biopsy.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with suspected GCA reports transient visual loss in one eye. What steroid regimen is appropriate?
options: IV methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g) then high-dose oral, with same-day ophthalmology
Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily, as for uncomplicated disease, with routine review
No steroids at all until the temporal artery biopsy result is available
Topical steroid eye drops, with oral treatment started only if vision worsens
A single low dose of oral steroid, repeated if the visual symptoms recur
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: IV methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g) then high-dose oral, with same-day ophthalmology
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Visual involvement in GCA warrants IV methylprednisolone (then oral) started immediately, with urgent ophthalmology, to protect the fellow eye.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Why is jaw claudication an important symptom in GCA?
options: It is a red flag for imminent visual loss (masticatory ischaemia)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: It is a red flag for imminent visual loss (masticatory ischaemia)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Jaw claudication (masticatory ischaemia) is a red flag for imminent visual loss in GCA.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What is the mechanism of vision loss in GCA?
options: Retinal detachment caused by traction from inflamed vitreous strands
Rapidly progressive cataract from the granulomatous inflammation itself
Vitreous haemorrhage from rupture of inflamed retinal vessels in the eye
Central retinal vein occlusion producing a stormy fundus and disc swelling
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (posterior ciliary artery occlusion → optic nerve ischaemia)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (posterior ciliary artery occlusion → optic nerve ischaemia)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Vision loss in GCA is due to anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy from posterior ciliary artery occlusion, giving a swollen pale disc; it is sudden, painless and irreversible.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which blood result is the key inflammatory finding in suspected GCA?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: ESR (markedly raised, often >50/>100)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: A markedly raised ESR and/or CRP is the key inflammatory finding - check both. Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude GCA, and treatment is never delayed for them.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A temporal artery biopsy is normal in a patient with a strong clinical picture of GCA. What is the correct interpretation?
options: GCA is not excluded — skip lesions can give a normal biopsy; treat on clinical grounds
Repeat the biopsy on the other side only
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: GCA is not excluded — skip lesions can give a normal biopsy; treat on clinical grounds
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Skip lesions make the biopsy patchy, so a normal biopsy does not exclude GCA; treatment is based on clinical suspicion.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What is the critical rule about treatment timing in GCA?
options: Do NOT delay steroids for investigations — start on clinical suspicion
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Do NOT delay steroids for investigations — start on clinical suspicion
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Steroids must be started immediately on clinical suspicion of GCA; the biopsy and ESR confirm the diagnosis afterwards.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which adjuncts are routinely given alongside long-term steroids in GCA?
options: Warfarin, to prevent thromboembolic visual loss
A statin, which suppresses the arterial inflammation
A proton pump inhibitor and bone protection (a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D)
Clopidogrel, in place of aspirin, for the duration of treatment
No adjunct is needed while the patient remains on prednisolone
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: A proton pump inhibitor and bone protection (a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Gastroprotection with a PPI and bone protection - a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D, started at the same time as the steroid without waiting for a DEXA - are routine. Routine antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is NOT recommended for GCA itself; aspirin is given only where there is a separate cardiovascular indication.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which biologic is used for relapsing or refractory GCA (or to reduce steroid exposure)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6) is used for relapsing/refractory GCA or as a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate is an alternative).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with GCA also reports bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, worse in the morning. What associated condition should be considered?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Polymyalgia rheumatica
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: GCA is strongly linked with polymyalgia rheumatica (girdle pain/stiffness); always screen for the other.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: An elderly patient started on long-term steroids for GCA needs which prophylaxis?
options: Bone protection (bisphosphonate + calcium + vitamin D) and a PPI
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Bone protection (bisphosphonate + calcium + vitamin D) and a PPI
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Long-term steroids in GCA require bone protection (bisphosphonate + calcium/vitamin D) and gastroprotection with a PPI.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Over what period are steroids typically tapered in GCA once controlled?
options: 1–2 years (slow wean guided by symptoms + ESR/CRP)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: 1–2 years (slow wean guided by symptoms + ESR/CRP)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Steroids in GCA are slowly weaned over 1–2 years, guided by symptoms and inflammatory markers.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What proportion of untreated GCA patients suffer permanent visual loss, underlining the urgency?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Around 15–20% of untreated GCA patients suffer permanent visual loss (AION), which is why immediate steroids are essential.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A 70-year-old presents with 3 weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, worst in the morning and taking over an hour to ease. Power is normal, ESR is raised and CK is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Polymyalgia rheumatica
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Bilateral girdle stiffness in the over-60s with a raised ESR, normal CK and no true weakness is polymyalgia rheumatica.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What is the crucial blood test that distinguishes PMR from polymyositis?
options: Creatine kinase (NORMAL in PMR, markedly raised in polymyositis)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Creatine kinase (NORMAL in PMR, markedly raised in polymyositis)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: CK is normal in PMR (stiffness, no true weakness) but markedly raised in polymyositis (true proximal weakness).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which associated condition must always be screened for in a patient with PMR?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Giant cell arteritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: PMR is strongly linked to giant cell arteritis (~15% develop GCA), so screen for headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual symptoms.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What response to treatment strongly supports a diagnosis of PMR?
options: A rapid, dramatic response to low-dose steroids (near-complete resolution within days)
A gradual, partial improvement developing slowly over several months
No change at all in the symptoms after a full trial of corticosteroids
A good response to NSAIDs alone, with no benefit from corticosteroids
A clear response to a course of antibiotics given for the systemic upset
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: A rapid, dramatic response to low-dose steroids (near-complete resolution within days)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: A dramatic response to low-dose steroids within days supports PMR; failure to respond should prompt reconsideration.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What is the first-line treatment for PMR?
options: Prednisolone 15 mg daily (with a slow taper over 1–2 years)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Prednisolone 15 mg daily (with a slow taper over 1–2 years)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: PMR is treated with prednisolone 15 mg daily (dramatic response), tapered slowly over 1–2 years.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with PMR is on long-term steroids. Which measures does the 'DON'T STOP' mnemonic emphasise?
options: Stop the steroids as soon as the girdle symptoms have fully improved
Bone protection alone, since that is the only significant steroid harm
A proton pump inhibitor alone, since gastric ulceration is the main risk
No special measures are needed at the low doses used in this condition
Don't stop abruptly (adrenal crisis), sick-day rules, treatment card, osteoporosis prevention and a PPI
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Don't stop abruptly (adrenal crisis), sick-day rules, treatment card, osteoporosis prevention and a PPI
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: 'DON'T STOP' covers not stopping abruptly, sick-day rules, a treatment card, osteoporosis prevention (bisphosphonate) and a PPI.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which feature would argue AGAINST a diagnosis of PMR and suggest myositis instead?
options: True proximal muscle weakness with a markedly raised CK
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: True proximal muscle weakness with a markedly raised CK
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: True proximal weakness with a raised CK suggests polymyositis, not PMR (which has stiffness, normal CK and no true weakness).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with suspected PMR has a normal ESR and does not respond to steroids. What should be considered?
options: Continue the steroids indefinitely and accept an incomplete response
Increase the steroids to a very high dose until the symptoms respond
Add antibiotics, since an occult infection is the commonest explanation
Reconsider the diagnosis and look for a mimic (e.g. fibromyalgia, myositis, malignancy)
Diagnose giant cell arteritis, which explains both the poor response and the normal ESR
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Reconsider the diagnosis and look for a mimic (e.g. fibromyalgia, myositis, malignancy)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: A normal ESR and no steroid response argue against PMR, prompting a search for a mimic such as fibromyalgia, myositis or malignancy.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What bone-related prophylaxis should be started immediately in a patient beginning long-term steroids for PMR?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: A bisphosphonate (alendronate) with calcium/vitamin D
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Bone protection (alendronate + calcium/vitamin D) should be started immediately with long-term steroids in PMR.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which duration of morning stiffness is characteristic of PMR?
options: Prolonged (≥45 min) in the shoulder and pelvic girdles
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Prolonged (≥45 min) in the shoulder and pelvic girdles
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Prolonged morning stiffness (≥45 min) in the shoulder and pelvic girdles is a hallmark of PMR.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which of the following is a differential that must be excluded in PMR (as it is a diagnosis of exclusion)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Myeloma (via protein electrophoresis)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Myeloma (screened with protein electrophoresis), along with rheumatoid, SLE, myositis, hyperparathyroidism and lung cancer, must be excluded in PMR.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient established on steroids for PMR becomes acutely unwell with an infection. What must NOT be done?
options: Stop the steroids abruptly (risking adrenal crisis)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Stop the steroids abruptly (risking adrenal crisis)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Steroids must never be stopped abruptly (risking adrenal crisis); when unwell, sick-day rules mean the dose is increased, not stopped.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which statement correctly summarises the PMR diagnostic picture?
options: Proximal weakness with a high CK and no response to corticosteroids
Small-joint synovitis with a positive rheumatoid factor and erosive change
A normal ESR with a normal CK and no response to a trial of steroids
Over 50 + bilateral girdle stiffness ≥45 min + normal CK + dramatic steroid response (usually with a raised ESR)
Distal weakness with a markedly raised CK and preserved proximal power
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Over 50 + bilateral girdle stiffness ≥45 min + normal CK + dramatic steroid response (usually with a raised ESR)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: PMR = over 60 + bilateral girdle pain/stiffness ≥45 min + raised ESR + normal CK + dramatic steroid response.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A middle-aged patient has chronic sinusitis, epistaxis, a collapsed nasal bridge (saddle nose), haemoptysis and haematuria with a rising creatinine. Which vasculitis is most likely?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: The ENT (saddle nose/sinusitis) + lung (haemoptysis) + kidney (glomerulonephritis) triad is granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which serology is highly specific for granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: cANCA (anti-PR3)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: cANCA (anti-proteinase-3) is highly specific for GPA (positive in ~90% of systemic disease).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which feature distinguishes GPA from microscopic polyangiitis (MPA)?
options: Both produce granulomas, so histology cannot separate them at all
MPA characteristically carries cANCA while GPA characteristically carries pANCA
GPA spares the kidneys entirely, whereas MPA causes glomerulonephritis
They are the same disease under two names and are managed identically
GPA has granulomas and prominent ENT involvement with cANCA/anti-PR3; MPA has no granulomas and pANCA/anti-MPO
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: GPA has granulomas and prominent ENT involvement with cANCA/anti-PR3; MPA has no granulomas and pANCA/anti-MPO
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: GPA has granulomas, prominent ENT disease and cANCA (anti-PR3); MPA lacks granulomas and is pANCA (anti-MPO).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A saddle-nose deformity in a patient with a systemic vasculitis results from what?
options: Direct trauma to the nose, which is the only recognised cause of the sign
Destruction of the nasal septum/cartilage by granulomatous inflammation
An allergic reaction causing chronic mucosal oedema and cartilage collapse
A congenital defect of septal cartilage unmasked by the systemic illness
Cocaine use, which is the only other cause and must always be excluded
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Destruction of the nasal septum/cartilage by granulomatous inflammation
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: In GPA, granulomatous inflammation destroys the nasal septum/cartilage, causing a collapsed bridge (saddle-nose deformity).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which renal biopsy finding is characteristic of GPA?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Necrotising, crescentic, pauci-immune glomerulonephritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: GPA causes a pauci-immune necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis on renal biopsy.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with GPA and organ-threatening disease needs induction. Which regimen is used?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: High-dose glucocorticoids + rituximab (or cyclophosphamide)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Induction for organ-threatening GPA is high-dose glucocorticoids + rituximab (preferred) or cyclophosphamide (>80% remission).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which vasculitis is characterised by asthma and eosinophilia, distinguishing it from GPA?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA/Churg-Strauss)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: EGPA (Churg-Strauss) features asthma and eosinophilia. pANCA (anti-MPO) is positive in only about a third of cases, so a negative ANCA does not exclude it.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with GPA is started on immunosuppression. Which prophylaxis is important (and also reduces relapse)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: PJP (pneumocystis) prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: PJP prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is important in GPA immunosuppression and also reduces relapse.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which set of investigations is most appropriate to screen the kidneys in suspected GPA?
options: Serum urate, since urate nephropathy is the mechanism of renal injury
Urinalysis (haematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts) and renal function
A DEXA scan, to assess the bone consequences of the renal involvement
Serum calcium and phosphate, to detect the mineral disturbance produced
An ECG, to detect the electrolyte disturbance of impaired renal function
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Urinalysis (haematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts) and renal function
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Urinalysis (looking for haematuria, proteinuria and red cell casts) and renal function screen for the glomerulonephritis of GPA.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which biologic is now preferred for both induction and maintenance in GPA?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Rituximab (anti-CD20)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Rituximab (anti-CD20) is now preferred for induction and maintenance in GPA (better safety, relapse and fertility outcomes).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with GPA in severe pulmonary haemorrhage may additionally receive which treatment?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Plasma exchange
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Plasma exchange is used in severe cases of GPA, such as severe pulmonary haemorrhage.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What is the natural history of untreated granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Rapidly fatal (necrotising glomerulonephritis + pulmonary haemorrhage)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Untreated GPA is rapidly fatal from necrotising glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage, so early aggressive treatment is essential.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A 28-year-old man from Turkey has recurrent painful mouth ulcers, genital ulcers and an episode of a painful red eye (uveitis). What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Behçet's disease
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Recurrent oral + genital ulcers with uveitis, in a patient from the Silk Road region, is Behçet's disease.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which HLA type is associated with Behçet's disease?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: HLA-B51
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Behçet's disease is associated with HLA-B51 (and the 'Silk Road' distribution).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What is the pathergy test in Behçet's disease?
options: A blood test for autoantibodies specific to the disease and its activity
A skin biopsy of an active lesion looking for a vasculitic infiltrate
An eye examination for the anterior uveitis that defines the condition
A needle prick to the forearm reviewed at 24–48h for erythema/induration (skin hypersensitivity)
A urine test for the inflammatory markers excreted during active disease
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: A needle prick to the forearm reviewed at 24–48h for erythema/induration (skin hypersensitivity)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: The pathergy test involves needle pricks to the skin reviewed at 24–48 hours for erythema/induration; positive results support Behçet's (also seen in Sweet's/pyoderma gangrenosum).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which feature of vascular involvement is characteristically unusual in Behçet's disease?
options: Involvement of BOTH arteries (aneurysms) AND veins (DVT, Budd-Chiari)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Involvement of BOTH arteries (aneurysms) AND veins (DVT, Budd-Chiari)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Behçet's is unusual in affecting both arteries (aneurysms) and veins (DVT, Budd-Chiari) — a prothrombotic variable-vessel vasculitis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: How is Behçet's disease diagnosed?
options: A single confirmatory blood test that is diagnostic when positive
Genetic testing for HLA-B51, which confirms the diagnosis on its own
Clinically — recurrent oral ulceration + ≥2 of genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions, or a positive pathergy test
Biopsy of an ulcer alone, which shows a characteristic histological appearance
Imaging of the large vessels alone, which shows the characteristic pattern
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Clinically — recurrent oral ulceration + ≥2 of genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions, or a positive pathergy test
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Behçet's is a clinical diagnosis based on recurrent oral ulcers plus ≥2 other features (genital ulcers, eye/skin lesions, positive pathergy).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which eye complication of Behçet's disease is sight-threatening and needs urgent ophthalmology?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Uveitis with retinal vasculitis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Uveitis with retinal vasculitis is a sight-threatening complication of Behçet's disease requiring urgent ophthalmology.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: What is first-line for mild mucocutaneous Behçet's disease?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Topical steroids/anaesthetics and colchicine
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Mild mucocutaneous Behçet's is managed with topical steroids/anaesthetics for ulcers and colchicine for mucocutaneous and joint symptoms.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with severe, refractory ocular and CNS Behçet's disease requires escalation. Which biologic is used?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Infliximab (anti-TNF)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Infliximab (anti-TNF) is used for severe/refractory Behçet's disease, especially eye, GI and CNS involvement, alongside steroids and azathioprine.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Which GI feature of Behçet's disease can mimic inflammatory bowel disease?
options: Ulceration of the ileum, caecum and ascending colon
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Ulceration of the ileum, caecum and ascending colon
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Behçet's causes ileocaecal/ascending colon ulceration that can mimic IBD (Crohn's).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: Describe the typical oral ulcers of Behçet's disease.
options: Painless, persistent ulcers that remain unchanged for many months
White plaques that can be scraped off to leave an erythematous base
Recurrent, painful, sharply circumscribed with a red halo, healing over 2–4 weeks
A single chronic ulcer with rolled, indurated edges that does not heal
Vesicular lesions that crust over and heal within a few days of onset
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: Recurrent, painful, sharply circumscribed with a red halo, healing over 2–4 weeks
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: Behçet's oral ulcers are recurrent (~3×/year), painful, sharply circumscribed with a red halo, healing over 2–4 weeks.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.question: A patient with Behçet's disease develops a DVT. How is the thrombosis best understood and managed?
options: A clotting factor deficiency; give factor replacement
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.answer: An inflammatory thrombosis; immunosuppression ± anticoagulation
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculit.explanation: The thrombosis in Behçet's is inflammatory, so management is immunosuppression ± anticoagulation (not anticoagulation alone).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which HLA type is associated with the seronegative spondyloarthropathies?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: The seronegative spondyloarthropathies are HLA-B27 associated (unlike rheumatoid arthritis, which is HLA-DR4).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A young man with inflammatory back pain that improves with exercise, sacroiliitis and a 'bamboo spine' has which spondyloarthropathy?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Axial inflammatory back pain with sacroiliitis and bamboo spine in a young man is ankylosing spondylitis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient develops arthritis 2 weeks after a bout of gastroenteritis, along with conjunctivitis and urethritis. Which condition is this?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Arthritis after a GI/GU infection with uveitis/conjunctivitis and urethritis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree') is reactive arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which extra-articular feature is shared across the spondyloarthropathies and needs urgent ophthalmology?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Anterior uveitis (a painful red eye) is a shared extra-articular feature of the spondyloarthropathies requiring same-day ophthalmology.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: How do the seronegative spondyloarthropathies differ from rheumatoid arthritis serologically?
options: They are RF/anti-CCP NEGATIVE (seronegative) and HLA-B27 associated
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: They are RF/anti-CCP NEGATIVE (seronegative) and HLA-B27 associated
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: The spondyloarthropathies are seronegative (RF/anti-CCP negative) and HLA-B27 associated, unlike seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A 25-year-old man has 6 months of gradually worsening lower back pain that is worst at night and in the morning, wakes him, lasts over an hour to ease, and improves when he exercises. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Gradual-onset inflammatory back pain in a young man (worse at rest/night, improves with movement, prolonged stiffness) is ankylosing spondylitis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which pattern best distinguishes inflammatory from mechanical back pain?
options: Worse with rest and at night, improves with movement, with prolonged morning stiffness
Worse with activity, relieved by rest
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Worse with rest and at night, improves with movement, with prolonged morning stiffness
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Inflammatory back pain is worse with rest/at night and improves with movement, with prolonged morning stiffness — the reverse of mechanical pain.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A young man with back pain develops a painful red eye with photophobia. Which extra-articular feature is this, and what is the action?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: A painful red eye in a young man with back pain is anterior uveitis (the commonest extra-articular feature of AS) requiring urgent ophthalmology.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which HLA allele is present in about 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Around 90% of ankylosing spondylitis patients are HLA-B27 positive (supportive, not diagnostic alone).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which test assesses lumbar spine mobility in suspected ankylosing spondylitis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Schober's test assesses lumbar flexion: with a 15 cm mark, an increase of less than 5 cm on bending forward indicates restricted mobility, supporting axial spondyloarthritis. The Thomas test is for fixed hip flexion deformity.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis develops sudden new severe neck pain after a minor fall. What must be assumed?
options: A simple muscle strain from the awkward movement during the fall
Ordinary mechanical neck pain, which is common after any minor injury
A flare of the anterior uveitis that commonly accompanies the disease
A spinal fracture (the fused 'bamboo spine' is brittle) until proven otherwise
Nothing serious, as the fused spine is more resistant to injury than normal
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: A spinal fracture (the fused 'bamboo spine' is brittle) until proven otherwise
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: New sudden neck/back pain in AS is a fracture until proven otherwise, because the fused bamboo spine is brittle.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which imaging modality detects EARLY sacroiliitis in ankylosing spondylitis before X-ray changes appear?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: MRI detects early sacroiliitis (bone marrow oedema) before X-ray changes, enabling earlier diagnosis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: What is the single most important (cornerstone) treatment for ankylosing spondylitis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Exercise and physiotherapy to maintain posture and spinal mobility is the cornerstone of AS management.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: What is the first-line drug treatment for ankylosing spondylitis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Regular NSAIDs are first-line; anti-TNF/anti-IL-17 are used for active disease inadequately controlled by NSAIDs.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Why are methotrexate and sulfasalazine of limited use in ankylosing spondylitis?
options: They are too toxic to use at the doses that axial disease would require
Conventional DMARDs do not work for AXIAL disease (only useful for peripheral joint involvement)
They precipitate anterior uveitis, the commonest extra-articular feature
They worsen inflammatory back pain by increasing spinal new bone formation
They are specifically contraindicated in anyone who is HLA-B27 positive
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Conventional DMARDs do not work for AXIAL disease (only useful for peripheral joint involvement)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Conventional DMARDs are ineffective for axial AS and are only useful for peripheral joint involvement.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which drug class is used for active ankylosing spondylitis not controlled by NSAIDs?
options: Conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate or sulfasalazine, given long term
Bisphosphonates, which suppress the new bone formation driving the fusion
Allopurinol, which lowers the urate that drives the entheseal inflammation
Colchicine, given long term to suppress the neutrophil-driven inflammation
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Anti-TNF or anti-IL-17 biologics are used for active axial disease that has not responded to two NSAIDs, each at the maximum tolerated dose over about 4 weeks, with objectively active disease. Screen for latent TB and hepatitis B/C before starting.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis develops an early diastolic murmur. Which of the 7 A's does this reflect?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Aortic regurgitation (from aortic root involvement) is one of the 7 A's of ankylosing spondylitis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which posture is characteristic of advanced ankylosing spondylitis?
options: Hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine with a compensatory flattened thorax
A fixed structural scoliosis with rib prominence on forward flexion
A 'question mark' posture (loss of lumbar lordosis, fixed thoracic kyphosis, hyperextended neck)
Posture is characteristically normal even in advanced, long-standing disease
An isolated forward head position with the rest of the spine unaffected
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: A 'question mark' posture (loss of lumbar lordosis, fixed thoracic kyphosis, hyperextended neck)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Progressive spinal fusion produces the 'question mark' posture — loss of lumbar lordosis, fixed thoracic kyphosis and a hyperextended neck.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis reports breathlessness. Which two mechanisms could explain this?
options: Anaemia of chronic disease alone, from the systemic inflammatory burden
Adult-onset asthma alone, as part of the extra-articular disease spectrum
Pulmonary embolism alone, from the immobility that the stiffness causes
A pleural effusion alone, from serosal inflammation of the pleural surface
Restricted chest wall expansion (costovertebral involvement) and apical lung fibrosis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Restricted chest wall expansion (costovertebral involvement) and apical lung fibrosis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Breathlessness in AS can be due to restricted chest wall expansion (costovertebral involvement) and apical lung fibrosis (one of the 7 A's).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient with plaque psoriasis develops pain and swelling of a whole finger ('sausage digit'), with nail pitting and DIP joint involvement. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Inflammatory arthritis with psoriasis, dactylitis, nail pitting and DIP involvement is psoriatic arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which feature distinguishes psoriatic arthritis from rheumatoid arthritis?
options: DIP joint involvement with nail changes, and seronegativity (RF/anti-CCP negative)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: DIP joint involvement with nail changes, and seronegativity (RF/anti-CCP negative)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Psoriatic arthritis affects the DIP joints (with nail disease) and is seronegative, unlike rheumatoid arthritis which spares the DIPs and is often seropositive.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which X-ray finding is the classic sign of psoriatic arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: The 'pencil-in-cup' deformity is the classic X-ray sign of psoriatic arthritis (arthritis mutilans). It is highly characteristic but also occurs in severe mutilating rheumatoid.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient with psoriatic arthritis has severe destruction of the phalanges with shortened, 'telescoping' digits. Which pattern is this?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Arthritis mutilans is the most severe pattern — osteolysis of the phalanges producing shortened, 'telescoping' digits.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which screening tool does NICE suggest for detecting psoriatic arthritis in patients with psoriasis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: The PEST tool is used to screen psoriasis patients for psoriatic arthritis, enabling early detection.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which two X-ray features together suggest psoriatic arthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Both erosion AND new bone formation (periostitis)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Both erosion AND new bone formation (periostitis)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Psoriatic arthritis shows both erosion and new bone formation (periostitis), whereas rheumatoid is purely erosive.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Nail pitting and onycholysis in psoriatic arthritis are strongly associated with disease of which joints?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Nail changes (pitting, onycholysis) strongly associate with DIP joint disease in psoriatic arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: What is the treatment for moderate-to-severe peripheral psoriatic arthritis, which also helps the skin?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Methotrexate is used for moderate/severe peripheral psoriatic arthritis and also treats the skin psoriasis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient has axial (spondylitis-pattern) psoriatic arthritis. Why won't methotrexate help the spine?
options: Methotrexate is simply too weak a drug to control spinal inflammation
Methotrexate worsens the psoriasis, so it cannot be used in these patients
Conventional DMARDs do not work for axial disease (only peripheral) → axial PsA needs NSAIDs/biologics
Methotrexate is contraindicated whenever the axial skeleton is involved
Methotrexate treats only the skin and has no effect on any joint disease
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Conventional DMARDs do not work for axial disease (only peripheral) → axial PsA needs NSAIDs/biologics
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Conventional DMARDs are ineffective for axial disease; axial PsA (like ankylosing spondylitis) needs NSAIDs or biologics.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient presents with an inflammatory arthritis and no obvious skin disease. Where should you examine for hidden psoriasis?
options: Only the palms, where pustular psoriasis characteristically hides
Only the face, where seborrhoeic-pattern psoriasis is easily overlooked
Only the soles, where plantar psoriasis is mistaken for simple callus
Psoriasis cannot be hidden — if there is no visible rash, there is none
The scalp, behind the ears, the umbilicus, the natal cleft and the nails
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: The scalp, behind the ears, the umbilicus, the natal cleft and the nails
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Psoriasis can be subtle/hidden in the scalp, behind the ears, the umbilicus, the natal cleft and the nails — examine these sites.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which biologic used in psoriatic arthritis targets IL-12/23 and also treats the skin?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Ustekinumab (anti-IL-12/23) is used in psoriatic arthritis and also treats the skin psoriasis; anti-TNF and anti-IL-17 are other options.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: What is the serology in psoriatic arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Psoriatic arthritis is seronegative (RF and anti-CCP negative), part of the seronegative spondyloarthropathy group.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which pattern of psoriatic arthritis most closely mimics rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Symmetrical polyarthritis; it resembles rheumatoid arthritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Symmetrical polyarthritis; it resembles rheumatoid arthritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: The symmetrical polyarthritis pattern most closely resembles rheumatoid arthritis — distinguished by the psoriasis and nail changes, DIP involvement and seronegativity.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A 25-year-old man develops an acutely swollen, painful knee 3 weeks after an episode of dysentery, along with conjunctivitis and urethritis. He is systemically well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Arthritis ~1–4 weeks after a GI/STI infection, with conjunctivitis and urethritis ('can't see, pee, climb a tree'), in a systemically well young man is reactive arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient presents with an acute hot swollen joint after gastroenteritis. Why must antibiotics be given after aspiration until investigations return?
options: Reactive arthritis itself requires a course of antibiotics to resolve
Antibiotics cure reactive arthritis by clearing organisms from the joint
To treat the associated anterior uveitis before it threatens vision
It is not necessary, since the two can be separated on clinical grounds
Because septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically and must be covered until aspiration excludes it
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Because septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically and must be covered until aspiration excludes it
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Reactive and septic arthritis cannot be distinguished clinically — fever does not separate them — so the joint is aspirated first and empirical antibiotics are then given until septic arthritis is excluded by culture.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which organism typically causes SEPTIC (not reactive) arthritis in a young sexually active patient?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) typically causes septic arthritis, whereas chlamydia is the classic genital trigger of reactive arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which is the classic genital trigger of reactive arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Chlamydia is the classic genital (STI) trigger of reactive arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which GI organisms are recognised triggers of reactive arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia and Campylobacter are the classic GI triggers of reactive arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: What does joint aspiration show in reactive arthritis?
options: Turbid fluid with organisms on culture
Sterile fluid with a high WBC and no organism (and no crystals)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Sterile fluid with a high WBC and no organism (and no crystals)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Reactive arthritis gives sterile synovial fluid with a high WBC and no organism (excluding septic and crystal arthritis).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Which skin sign of reactive arthritis appears as waxy papules on the palms and soles?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Keratoderma blennorrhagica (waxy yellow/brown papules on palms/soles) is a skin sign of reactive arthritis; circinate balanitis affects the penis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: What is the first-line treatment for the joint symptoms of reactive arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: NSAIDs are first-line for the joint symptoms of reactive arthritis; the trigger is treated and septic arthritis excluded first.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient has reactive arthritis triggered by chlamydia. What management is important regarding the trigger?
options: Treat the chlamydia (and the sexual partner)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Treat the chlamydia (and the sexual partner)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: The triggering chlamydia infection should be treated, including partner treatment for the STI.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: A patient with reactive arthritis develops a painful red eye. What is the appropriate action?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: A painful red eye (anterior uveitis) in reactive arthritis needs urgent ophthalmology; conjunctivitis is the milder eye involvement.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: What is the usual prognosis of reactive arthritis?
options: Most resolve within about 6 months and do not recur
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.answer: Most resolve within about 6 months and do not recur
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Most cases of reactive arthritis resolve within ~6 months without recurrence; recurrent/chronic disease may need DMARDs or anti-TNF.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.question: Reactive arthritis is more common in which condition, which should be excluded?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Seronega.explanation: Reactive arthritis is more common in HIV, which should be excluded as part of the work-up.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A 45-year-old woman has 3 months of symmetrical pain, swelling and stiffness in the small joints of both hands, worst in the morning and lasting over an hour, improving as she uses her hands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Symmetrical small-joint arthritis with prolonged morning stiffness that improves with use is the inflammatory pattern of rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which hand joints are characteristically SPARED in rheumatoid arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis spares the DIP joints (DIP involvement suggests osteoarthritis) — a key hand discriminator.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which autoantibody is MORE specific than rheumatoid factor and may pre-date the disease?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Anti-CCP is far more specific than rheumatoid factor (sensitivity is similar), often pre-dates disease onset and predicts more erosive disease.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Rheumatoid factor is typically an antibody of which type, directed against what?
options: IgM against the Fc portion of the patient's own IgG
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: IgM against the Fc portion of the patient's own IgG
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Rheumatoid factor is usually an IgM autoantibody against the Fc portion of the patient's own IgG.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: The destructive, tumour-like proliferation of inflamed synovium that erodes cartilage and bone in rheumatoid arthritis is called what?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: The pannus is the proliferating inflamed synovium that grows over and destroys cartilage and subchondral bone in rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A hand deformity with a hyperextended PIP joint and flexed DIP joint is called what?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Swan-neck deformity is hyperextension of the PIP with flexion of the DIP; boutonnière is the opposite (flexed PIP, hyperextended DIP).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is due for surgery requiring intubation. Which complication must be assessed for beforehand, and how?
options: Atlantoaxial subluxation; cervical spine flexion–extension X-rays (MRI if abnormal)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: Atlantoaxial subluxation; cervical spine flexion–extension X-rays (MRI if abnormal)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Atlantoaxial subluxation (C1/C2) can cause cord compression during neck manipulation for intubation, so flexion–extension cervical spine X-rays are done pre-operatively, with MRI if abnormal or if there are neurological signs.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has splenomegaly and a low neutrophil count. What is this syndrome called?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Felty's syndrome = rheumatoid arthritis + splenomegaly + low WCC/neutropenia.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A coal miner with rheumatoid arthritis has multiple pulmonary nodules on chest X-ray. What is this called?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Caplan's syndrome = rheumatoid nodules + pneumoconiosis (coal dust or silica exposure).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which set of X-ray features characterises rheumatoid arthritis (the LESS mnemonic)?
options: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Sclerosis, Cysts
Loss of joint space, Erosions, Soft-tissue swelling, Soft bones (osteopenia)
Loss of density, Erosions, Sclerosis, Spurs
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: Loss of joint space, Erosions, Soft-tissue swelling, Soft bones (osteopenia)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Rheumatoid = LESS (Loss of joint space, Erosions, Soft-tissue swelling, Soft bones/osteopenia); osteoarthritis = LOSS (osteophytes/sclerosis).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which DMARD is the usual first choice — the 'anchor drug' — in rheumatoid arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Methotrexate is the usual anchor DMARD, given once weekly with folic acid. Leflunomide and sulfasalazine are the alternative first-line monotherapies; hydroxychloroquine is reserved for mild or palindromic disease.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has failed two DMARDs including methotrexate. Which treatment is next, and what must be checked first?
options: A TNF-α inhibitor; screen for latent TB (interferon-gamma release assay and CXR) and for hepatitis first
A repeat course of the same two DMARDs at the same doses, given for longer this time
Long-term high-dose oral steroids as the definitive maintenance treatment from now on
No further disease-modifying treatment — move to analgesia and joint protection only
Regular paracetamol alone, with review only if the joints become deformed over time
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: A TNF-α inhibitor; screen for latent TB (interferon-gamma release assay and CXR) and for hepatitis first
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: After ≥2 failed DMARDs (including methotrexate), a TNF-α inhibitor is used. A chest X-ray alone misses latent TB, so an interferon-gamma release assay is done as well, with hepatitis B/C screening.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which blood tests must be monitored in a patient on methotrexate?
options: Serum urate and calcium, checked before starting and then at each dose increase
Thyroid function tests, since methotrexate commonly precipitates hypothyroidism
FBC, LFTs and U&E (myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity and renal excretion)
Serum amylase, because pancreatitis is the main dose-limiting toxicity of the drug
Morning cortisol, to detect the adrenal suppression that methotrexate can produce
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: FBC, LFTs and U&E (myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity and renal excretion)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Methotrexate needs FBC, LFT and U&E monitoring — it is renally excreted, and falling renal function is the commonest precipitant of toxicity. It is also teratogenic.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which vaccine type should be AVOIDED in a patient on immunosuppression for rheumatoid arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Live vaccines are avoided in immunosuppressed patients; annual influenza and a one-off pneumococcal (inactivated) vaccination are recommended, ideally before immunosuppression starts.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which scoring tool is used to monitor rheumatoid arthritis disease activity and treatment response?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: The DAS28 (28 joints: swollen + tender + ESR/CRP) monitors disease activity and treatment response; HAQ assesses function.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A woman has recurrent episodes of joint inflammation lasting a few days that fully resolve, with positive anti-CCP. What is this, and its significance?
options: Palindromic rheumatism; may progress to established rheumatoid arthritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: Palindromic rheumatism; may progress to established rheumatoid arthritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Palindromic rheumatism (self-limiting episodes) with positive rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP may progress to established rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which extra-articular feature is a leading cause of death in rheumatoid arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis accelerates atherosclerosis, increasing cardiovascular disease risk — a leading cause of death.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A patient develops progressive, boring, severe eye pain, redness and reduced vision. Which serious ocular complication of rheumatoid arthritis is this?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Scleritis is a serious, painful ocular complication of rheumatoid arthritis (episcleritis is milder); it threatens vision.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Within what timeframe should an adult with suspected persistent synovitis be referred to rheumatology (NICE)?
options: Only once rheumatoid factor is positive
Urgently — within 3 working days of presentation
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: Urgently — within 3 working days of presentation
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: NICE advises urgent referral within 3 working days of presentation, and referral should not be delayed for normal inflammatory markers or negative serology.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has a joint aspirate that is turbid with a high leucocyte count, a negative Gram stain and no crystals. What do these findings make less likely?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis, which characteristically gives a clear, low-cell-count aspirate
Septic arthritis and crystal arthritis — though culture is still needed to exclude infection
Osteoarthritis, which cannot produce an effusion with a raised white cell count
Reactive arthritis, which is excluded by the absence of organisms on Gram stain
Nothing at all — a synovial fluid analysis carries no diagnostic value in this setting
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: Septic arthritis and crystal arthritis — though culture is still needed to exclude infection
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: These findings argue against septic and crystal arthritis — but a negative Gram stain does NOT exclude infection (it is only around 50% sensitive). Await culture and treat empirically if septic arthritis is suspected.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which pattern of joint involvement is typical of rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis (MCP, PIP, wrist, MTP)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: Symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis (MCP, PIP, wrist, MTP)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis causes a symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis (MCP, PIP, wrist, MTP), sparing the DIP joints.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Why is smoking a risk factor specifically linked to anti-CCP-positive rheumatoid arthritis?
options: It promotes citrullination of proteins, generating anti-CCP antibodies
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: It promotes citrullination of proteins, generating anti-CCP antibodies
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Smoking promotes citrullination of proteins, driving anti-CCP (ACPA) antibody formation — linking it to seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A patient with early rheumatoid arthritis is started on methotrexate. Why is a short course of prednisolone often given at the same time?
options: As a short-course 'bridging' therapy to control symptoms until the DMARD takes effect
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: As a short-course 'bridging' therapy to control symptoms until the DMARD takes effect
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Bridging corticosteroids control symptoms rapidly while the slower-acting DMARD takes effect. They are given as a SHORT course only — long-term steroids risk osteoporosis, diabetes and infection.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which deformity involves flexion of the PIP joint and hyperextension of the DIP joint?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Boutonnière deformity is flexion of the PIP with hyperextension of the DIP (the reverse of swan-neck).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: What is the overarching treatment strategy in rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Symptom relief with NSAIDs alone, reserving DMARDs for established joint deformity
Treat-to-target — early DMARDs escalated to achieve remission/low disease activity (monitored by DAS28)
Waiting until deformities have developed before committing the patient to treatment
Long-term corticosteroids alone, titrated against the patient's symptoms over time
Early joint replacement surgery first-line, with drug treatment reserved for failures
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.answer: Treat-to-target — early DMARDs escalated to achieve remission/low disease activity (monitored by DAS28)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is managed treat-to-target: early DMARDs escalated (monitored by DAS28) to reach remission before irreversible damage.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: Which HLA type is associated with rheumatoid arthritis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis (HLA-B27 is associated with the seronegative spondyloarthropathies).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops progressive breathlessness with bibasal fibrosis on imaging. Which extra-articular complication is this?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumato.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis can cause pulmonary fibrosis (interstitial lung disease), along with nodules, effusions and Caplan's syndrome.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A 60-year-old has knee pain that is worse after walking and at the end of the day, with only a few minutes of morning stiffness and no systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Osteoarthritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Activity-related pain worse at the end of the day with brief morning stiffness and no systemic features is osteoarthritis (a mechanical/degenerative pattern).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Which hand joint finding distinguishes osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis?
options: DIP involvement (Heberden's nodes) — rheumatoid spares the DIP joints
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: DIP involvement (Heberden's nodes) — rheumatoid spares the DIP joints
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: OA affects the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes), which rheumatoid arthritis characteristically spares — a key hand discriminator.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Bony swellings at the DIP joints in osteoarthritis are called what?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Heberden's nodes
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Heberden's nodes are at the DIP joints ('Heberden's = Higher'); Bouchard's nodes are at the PIP joints.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Which four X-ray features characterise osteoarthritis (the LOSS mnemonic)?
options: Loss of joint space, Osteopenia, Sclerosis, Swelling
Loss of density, Osteopenia, Sclerosis, Cysts
Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: LOSS = Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: According to NICE, when can osteoarthritis be diagnosed clinically without investigations?
options: In anyone presenting with joint pain of any kind, regardless of their age, the pattern of the pain or the joints involved
If the patient is aged 45 or over, has activity-related joint pain, and has no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting no more than 30 minutes
Only once a plain X-ray has confirmed loss of joint space and osteophyte formation
Only once blood tests have shown normal inflammatory markers and no autoantibodies
Never — a confident diagnosis of osteoarthritis always requires imaging of the affected joint, whatever the history suggests
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: If the patient is aged 45 or over, has activity-related joint pain, and has no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting no more than 30 minutes
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: OA can be diagnosed clinically in a patient aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and no morning stiffness (or stiffness lasting no longer than 30 minutes); investigate only if atypical.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: What is the first-line (core) treatment for osteoarthritis?
options: A strong opioid such as morphine, titrated against the severity of the joint pain
Immediate referral for joint replacement, before any conservative measures are tried
A course of systemic corticosteroids to suppress the inflammation within the joint
Non-pharmacological measures — exercise for everyone, plus education and weight management
Methotrexate, to slow the structural progression of cartilage loss within the joint
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Non-pharmacological measures — exercise for everyone, plus education and weight management
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: The core first-line treatment is non-pharmacological — therapeutic exercise for everyone, with education and weight management for those living with overweight or obesity.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for knee osteoarthritis (NICE)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: A topical NSAID
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: NICE recommends topical NSAIDs first-line, especially for the knee. Paracetamol and weak opioids should not be routinely offered, and strong opioids should not be offered at all.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A patient with severe hip osteoarthritis has ongoing pain and loss of function despite conservative measures. What is the definitive treatment?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Total hip replacement
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Total hip (or knee) replacement is considered when joint symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical management is ineffective or unsuitable. Referral must not be restricted by age, sex, smoking, comorbidity or obesity (NICE).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: What do inflammatory markers and autoantibodies typically show in osteoarthritis?
options: Raised CRP and positive rheumatoid factor
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Normal (normal inflammatory markers, no autoantibodies)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: In OA, inflammatory markers are normal and there are no autoantibodies (unlike rheumatoid arthritis).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Which finding best fits rheumatoid arthritis rather than osteoarthritis?
options: Pain that is worse with activity and towards the end of the working day
Prolonged morning stiffness (>30–60 min), symmetrical MCP/wrist involvement and systemic features
Heberden's nodes — bony swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints of the hand
Brief morning stiffness lasting only a few minutes and easing as the patient moves
Distal interphalangeal joint involvement with squaring at the base of the thumb
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Prolonged morning stiffness (>30–60 min), symmetrical MCP/wrist involvement and systemic features
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis has prolonged morning stiffness, symmetrical small-joint (MCP/wrist) involvement and systemic features; OA is mechanical with brief stiffness and DIP involvement.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Why should treatment in osteoarthritis be guided by symptoms rather than the X-ray?
options: Plain X-rays are technically unreliable and frequently misread by non-radiologists
X-rays are contraindicated in osteoarthritis because of the cumulative radiation dose
The symptoms are irrelevant — only the radiographic grade should guide the treatment
X-ray changes correlate poorly with symptoms (severe changes can be asymptomatic and vice versa) → treat the patient, not the X-ray
X-rays always overestimate disease severity, so their findings should be discounted
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: X-ray changes correlate poorly with symptoms (severe changes can be asymptomatic and vice versa) → treat the patient, not the X-ray
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: X-ray changes correlate poorly with symptoms in OA, so management is guided by the patient's symptoms and function.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Which analgesic approach should NOT be offered in osteoarthritis?
options: A topical NSAID for knee pain
Paracetamol used infrequently for short-term relief
An oral NSAID at the lowest effective dose with gastroprotection
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Strong opioids
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Strong opioids should not be offered in OA. Management centres on exercise and weight management with topical, then oral, NSAIDs, and joint replacement for severe disease.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A 68-year-old woman has deep, aching hip pain that worsens when she walks and settles with rest, with pain radiating to the groin and reduced internal rotation. X-ray shows joint-space loss and osteophytes. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Hip osteoarthritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Activity-related groin pain with reduced internal rotation and radiographic joint-space loss/osteophytes is hip osteoarthritis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A 55-year-old obese labourer has bilateral knee pain worse at the end of the working day, with crepitus and bony swelling but no warmth or systemic upset. Which risk factors are most relevant here?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Obesity and occupational joint loading
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Obesity and occupational joint loading are major risk factors for osteoarthritis (along with age, female sex and family history).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: On examination of a patient with hand osteoarthritis, which combination of signs would you expect?
options: MCP swelling, ulnar deviation and wrist involvement
Heberden's nodes (DIP), Bouchard's nodes (PIP) and squaring of the thumb base (CMC)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Heberden's nodes (DIP), Bouchard's nodes (PIP) and squaring of the thumb base (CMC)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Hand OA classically shows Heberden's (DIP) and Bouchard's (PIP) nodes with CMC thumb-base squaring.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A grating sensation felt (and sometimes heard) when moving an osteoarthritic joint is called what?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Crepitus
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Crepitus is the grating sensation on movement of an osteoarthritic joint, from the roughened joint surfaces.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Which single feature most reliably distinguishes osteoarthritis from an inflammatory arthritis on history?
options: Pain worse with activity and only brief (<30 min) morning stiffness
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Pain worse with activity and only brief (<30 min) morning stiffness
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: A mechanical pattern — pain worse with activity and brief morning stiffness (<30 min) — best distinguishes OA from inflammatory arthritis (rest pain, prolonged stiffness).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A patient with severe knee osteoarthritis is keen to avoid surgery and has ongoing pain despite topical NSAIDs. Which option provides short-term symptomatic relief?
options: A strong opioid taken long-term, titrated upwards as the joint pain progresses
A course of systemic corticosteroids to suppress inflammation throughout the joint
An intra-articular corticosteroid injection (relief lasting roughly 2 to 10 weeks)
Methotrexate, to slow the structural progression of cartilage loss within the knee
Allopurinol, to reduce the crystal deposition that drives the degenerative change
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: An intra-articular corticosteroid injection (relief lasting roughly 2 to 10 weeks)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: An intra-articular corticosteroid injection gives short-term relief only — roughly 2 to 10 weeks — and is used when other drug treatments are unsuitable or to support the person to exercise. Strong opioids are not offered and DMARDs are not used.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A patient with knee osteoarthritis asks whether they should rest the joint. What is the best advice?
options: Complete rest and avoidance of all activity until the knee pain has fully settled
Immobilisation of the knee in a cast so that the damaged cartilage can recover
Use of a wheelchair to keep weight off the joint and prevent further cartilage loss
Avoidance of physiotherapy, since strengthening work accelerates joint degeneration
Regular exercise (muscle strengthening + aerobic) is a core treatment that improves pain and function
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Regular exercise (muscle strengthening + aerobic) is a core treatment that improves pain and function
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Exercise (strengthening + aerobic) is a core first-line treatment in OA, improving pain and function — rest is not advised.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A 50-year-old presents with pain and squaring at the base of the thumb, worse with gripping. Which joint is affected?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: The first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Squaring at the thumb base reflects OA of the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Which statement about blood tests in osteoarthritis is correct?
options: ESR and CRP are markedly raised
Inflammatory markers and autoantibodies are normal
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Inflammatory markers and autoantibodies are normal
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: In OA the inflammatory markers are normal and there are no autoantibodies; abnormal results should prompt consideration of another diagnosis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A 47-year-old has typical activity-related knee pain with no morning stiffness. According to NICE, what is the appropriate diagnostic approach?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Diagnose osteoarthritis clinically without investigations
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: In a patient aged 45 or over with activity-related pain and no morning stiffness, OA is diagnosed clinically without investigations.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A patient has marked osteophytes and joint-space loss on knee X-ray but only mild symptoms, while another has severe pain with only minor radiographic changes. What principle does this illustrate?
options: X-ray changes correlate poorly with symptoms — treat the patient, not the X-ray
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: X-ray changes correlate poorly with symptoms — treat the patient, not the X-ray
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: Radiographic severity correlates poorly with symptoms in OA, so treatment is guided by the patient's symptoms and function.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: Which set of joints is characteristically affected by osteoarthritis?
options: Only the small joints of the hands symmetrically
Only the MCP joints and wrists
Weight-bearing joints (knees, hips), hands (DIP/PIP/CMC), spine and the first MTP
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: Weight-bearing joints (knees, hips), hands (DIP/PIP/CMC), spine and the first MTP
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: OA typically affects weight-bearing joints (knees, hips), the hands (DIP/PIP/CMC), the spine and the first MTP joint.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.question: A patient with a hot, acutely swollen, exquisitely tender single joint is being assessed. Why is this unlikely to be simple osteoarthritis?
options: Osteoarthritis never affects that joint, so the diagnosis must be something else
OA is not acutely hot and inflamed — an acute hot joint requires exclusion of septic arthritis or crystal arthritis
Osteoarthritis always causes a fever, and the absence of one excludes the diagnosis
Osteoarthritis causes symmetrical swelling only, never a single affected joint
Osteoarthritis cannot cause pain of this severity at any stage of the disease
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.answer: OA is not acutely hot and inflamed — an acute hot joint requires exclusion of septic arthritis or crystal arthritis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoart.explanation: OA is a chronic mechanical process, not an acutely hot inflamed joint; an acute hot joint needs septic/crystal arthritis excluded (aspirate).
