Serum albumin as a negative acute-phase reactant
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.explanation: Ferritin is markedly raised (often >1000 micrograms/L or more than five times the upper limit of normal) and is the acute-phase marker of choice for monitoring AOSD activity. A low glycosylated fraction adds specificity but is a specialist assay.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.question: Which malignancy is the most important to exclude, as it can mimic adult-onset Still's disease exactly?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.explanation: Lymphoma can mimic AOSD exactly and must be excluded, along with other infection and autoimmune causes.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.question: A patient with AOSD is not controlled on NSAIDs. What is the next step in management?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-On.explanation: The escalation is NSAIDs → corticosteroids → DMARDs/biologics (methotrexate, IL-1/IL-6 inhibitors, anti-TNF) for persistent disease.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A muscle is striated, multinucleate and under voluntary control, contracting quickly and forcefully but fatiguing. Which type is it?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Skeletal muscle
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Striated, multinucleate, voluntary muscle that contracts fast but fatigues is skeletal muscle.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which structural feature allows cardiac muscle to contract as a coordinated functional syncytium?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Intercalated discs containing gap junctions
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Intercalated discs with gap junctions electrically couple cardiac cells, so they contract together as a syncytium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Why can cardiac muscle not be tetanised?
options: It has a long refractory period (the Ca²⁺ plateau)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: It has a long refractory period (the Ca²⁺ plateau)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: The long cardiac refractory period prevents summation, so the ventricle relaxes and refills between beats rather than contracting continuously.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: An endurance athlete has a predominance of slow, fatigue-resistant, aerobic, mitochondria-rich muscle fibres. Which fibre type is this?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Type I (slow-twitch)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Type I (slow-twitch) fibres are slow, fatigue-resistant and aerobic, suited to endurance and posture.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Smooth muscle triggers contraction using which calcium-binding protein, distinguishing it from striated muscle?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Calmodulin (activating myosin light-chain kinase)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Smooth muscle uses calmodulin (Ca²⁺-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase), whereas striated muscle uses troponin.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which feature is unique to cardiac (not skeletal) muscle?
options: Cross-striations visible on light microscopy of the muscle fibre
Voluntary control exerted through the somatic motor nervous system
Multinucleate fibres formed by the fusion of many precursor myoblasts
Intrinsic pacemaker automaticity (SA node) with a long refractory period
Use of troponin as the calcium-sensing protein of the thin filament
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Intrinsic pacemaker automaticity (SA node) with a long refractory period
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Cardiac muscle has intrinsic automaticity (SA node) and a long refractory period; skeletal muscle needs nerve stimulation and can tetanise.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which muscle type maintains sustained tone at low energy cost via a 'latch mechanism', e.g. in blood vessels and sphincters?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Smooth muscle
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Smooth muscle uses the latch mechanism to maintain tone tirelessly at low energy cost (e.g. vascular tone, sphincters).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Compared with skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle contraction is more dependent on which calcium source?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Extracellular calcium (Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Cardiac muscle uses Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release and is more dependent on extracellular calcium than skeletal muscle.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which muscle type is arranged as single-unit (e.g. gut, bladder) or multi-unit (e.g. iris, large airways)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Smooth muscle
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Smooth muscle is classified as single-unit (gap-junction-coupled sheets) or multi-unit (individually controlled).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient has rhabdomyolysis after a crush injury, with myoglobinuria, acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia. Which muscle type has broken down?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Skeletal muscle
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Rhabdomyolysis is breakdown of skeletal muscle, releasing myoglobin (→ AKI) and potassium (→ hyperkalaemia).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from a defect in which structural protein of which muscle type?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Dystrophin in skeletal muscle
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Muscular dystrophies are skeletal muscle structural protein defects — Duchenne is caused by a dystrophin defect.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: What is the single mechanism by which all three muscle types generate force?
options: Calcium-triggered sliding of actin and myosin filaments
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Calcium-triggered sliding of actin and myosin filaments
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: All three muscle types contract by the calcium-triggered sliding-filament mechanism; they differ only in the details of control and calcium handling.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: During muscle contraction, what physically happens to the actin and myosin filaments?
options: The filaments slide past each other, shortening the sarcomere
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: The filaments slide past each other, shortening the sarcomere
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: In the sliding-filament mechanism the filaments slide past one another (they do not shorten), shortening the sarcomere.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: At rest, what prevents actin and myosin from binding, and how is this overcome?
options: Titin blocks the site; ATP removes it
Myosin heads are absent; nerve stimulation adds them
The Z-line blocks it; the AP removes it
Dystrophin blocks it; calcium removes it
Tropomyosin blocks the binding site; calcium binding troponin moves it aside
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Tropomyosin blocks the binding site; calcium binding troponin moves it aside
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Tropomyosin blocks the actin-myosin binding site at rest; calcium binds troponin, moving tropomyosin aside to allow contraction.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: In excitation-contraction coupling, what triggers calcium release into the cytoplasm?
options: ATP binding to the myosin head and releasing it from the actin filament
The action potential travelling down the T-tubules triggering the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium
Calcium entering the cytoplasm from the bone mineral reservoir in the skeleton
Tropomyosin binding to actin and exposing the myosin-binding sites directly
The power stroke of the myosin head pulling the thin filament inwards
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: The action potential travelling down the T-tubules triggering the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: The AP spreads down the T-tubules and triggers the SR to release its stored calcium into the cytoplasm.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which two things are essential for the cross-bridge cycle to proceed?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Calcium (the trigger) and ATP (the fuel)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Calcium triggers the cycle (exposing binding sites via troponin) and ATP fuels it (power stroke and detachment).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Why does rigor mortis occur after death?
options: ATP runs out, so myosin cannot detach from actin and the muscles stay rigidly contracted
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: ATP runs out, so myosin cannot detach from actin and the muscles stay rigidly contracted
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Without ATP, myosin cannot detach from actin, so muscles remain rigidly contracted — rigor mortis (the 'ATP for detachment' illustration).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient develops a rapid rise in temperature, muscle rigidity and rising CO₂ after a volatile anaesthetic and suxamethonium. What is the mechanism and treatment?
options: A ryanodine-receptor defect causing uncontrolled SR calcium release; dantrolene
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: A ryanodine-receptor defect causing uncontrolled SR calcium release; dantrolene
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is a ryanodine-receptor (SR calcium-release channel) defect causing massive uncontrolled calcium release; dantrolene blocks calcium release.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Why is muscle RELAXATION considered an active, ATP-requiring process?
options: It needs ATP to break actin
Calcium must be actively pumped back into the SR by a Ca²⁺-ATPase
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Calcium must be actively pumped back into the SR by a Ca²⁺-ATPase
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Relaxation requires ATP to pump calcium back into the SR (via a Ca²⁺-ATPase); this is why ATP depletion prevents relaxation.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: How does cardiac excitation-contraction coupling differ from skeletal?
options: Cardiac contraction does not use calcium, relying on sodium influx instead
It requires extracellular calcium entry to trigger SR calcium release (calcium-induced calcium release)
It uses calmodulin rather than troponin C as the calcium-binding protein
Cardiac muscle has no T-tubules, so calcium diffuses in from the surface only
Cardiac contraction does not require ATP, being driven by the pacemaker alone
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: It requires extracellular calcium entry to trigger SR calcium release (calcium-induced calcium release)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Cardiac muscle depends on extracellular calcium entry (during the plateau) to trigger SR calcium release — calcium-induced calcium release.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: During the power stroke of the cross-bridge cycle, what happens?
options: ATP binds the myosin head, which then detaches from the actin filament
The myosin head re-cocks into its high-energy configuration ready to bind
Calcium is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by SERCA
The myosin head pivots and pulls the actin filament inward, releasing ADP and Pi
Tropomyosin slides back to block the myosin-binding sites on actin
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: The myosin head pivots and pulls the actin filament inward, releasing ADP and Pi
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: In the power stroke the myosin head pivots, pulling actin inward and shortening the sarcomere, with release of ADP and Pi.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which drug blocks SR calcium release and is used in malignant hyperthermia?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Dantrolene
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Dantrolene blocks SR calcium release and is the treatment for malignant hyperthermia (and used in spasticity).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A structural protein linking the sarcomere to the cell membrane is defective, causing progressive muscle damage. Which protein and disease?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Dystrophin; Duchenne muscular dystrophy
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Dystrophin links the sarcomere to the membrane; its defect causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: What immediately triggers calcium binding to expose the actin binding sites in skeletal muscle?
options: Calcium binding to troponin, which moves tropomyosin aside
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Calcium binding to troponin, which moves tropomyosin aside
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Calcium binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the actin binding sites, allowing myosin to bind and contraction to begin.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: At the neuromuscular junction, what event directly triggers acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal?
options: Calcium influx through voltage-gated channels when the AP arrives
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Calcium influx through voltage-gated channels when the AP arrives
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: The arriving AP opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; the Ca²⁺ influx triggers vesicles to release ACh into the cleft.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which enzyme terminates transmission at the neuromuscular junction?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Acetylcholinesterase
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh in the cleft, terminating the signal.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A woman has ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day and with repeated activity, and a chest CT shows a thymoma. What is the defect?
options: Antibodies blocking/destroying postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Antibodies blocking/destroying postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Fatiguable weakness worse with use, with thymoma, is myasthenia gravis — antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A man with small cell lung cancer has proximal weakness that IMPROVES with repeated use. What is the diagnosis and mechanism?
options: Myasthenia gravis; postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies
Botulism; presynaptic blockade of acetylcholine release from the terminal
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome; antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels reducing ACh release
Organophosphate poisoning; excess acetylcholine causing depolarising block
Duchenne muscular dystrophy; a defect in the dystrophin structural protein
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome; antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels reducing ACh release
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Weakness improving with use plus small cell lung cancer is Lambert-Eaton syndrome — anti-presynaptic Ca²⁺ channel antibodies reducing ACh release.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Why does pyridostigmine (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) help in myasthenia gravis?
options: It destroys the antibodies directed against the acetylcholine receptor
It blocks presynaptic calcium channels and so reduces acetylcholine release
It relaxes the muscle directly, relieving the sensation of fatigable weakness
It reduces acetylcholine release, resetting the sensitivity of the receptors
It increases ACh in the cleft, giving more chance to bind the reduced receptors
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: It increases ACh in the cleft, giving more chance to bind the reduced receptors
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: By inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, pyridostigmine raises ACh in the cleft, improving binding to the reduced receptor population.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient develops flaccid paralysis after botulinum toxin exposure. What is the mechanism?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Blocked ACh release (presynaptic)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release presynaptically, causing flaccid paralysis (botulism); the same mechanism is used therapeutically as botulinum toxin type A.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A farmer presents with excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, muscle fasciculations and weakness after pesticide exposure. What is the mechanism and treatment?
options: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition (↑↑ACh, cholinergic crisis); atropine + pralidoxime
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition (↑↑ACh, cholinergic crisis); atropine + pralidoxime
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing a cholinergic crisis (SLUDGE + fasciculations); treatment is atropine + pralidoxime.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which muscle relaxant causes initial fasciculations then paralysis and is NOT reversed by neostigmine?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Suxamethonium (a depolarising blocker)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Suxamethonium is a depolarising blocker that activates then blocks the receptor; anticholinesterases worsen it, so it is not reversed by neostigmine.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which agent reverses rocuronium (a non-depolarising blocker) by binding it directly?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Sugammadex
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Sugammadex binds rocuronium directly to reverse it; non-depolarising blockers are also reversible with neostigmine (which raises ACh).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which caution applies specifically to suxamethonium?
options: It causes hyperkalaemia and can trigger malignant hyperthermia
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: It causes hyperkalaemia and can trigger malignant hyperthermia
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Suxamethonium causes hyperkalaemia (the risk after burns or crush injury develops from about 24-48 hours and persists for months) and can trigger malignant hyperthermia.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: What underlies the NMJ's reliability, whereby one nerve AP normally always triggers one muscle AP?
options: A large safety margin — far more ACh is released than needed
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: A large safety margin — far more ACh is released than needed
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: The NMJ has a large safety margin (excess ACh release), so one nerve AP reliably triggers one muscle AP; diseases erode this margin.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which contrast between botulinum toxin and organophosphates is correct?
options: Both toxins increase acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing a depolarising block
Both toxins decrease acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing a flaccid paralysis
Botulinum inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates in the cleft
Botulinum decreases ACh (blocks release), organophosphates increase ACh (block breakdown) — opposite mechanisms, both causing weakness
Organophosphates block acetylcholine release from the presynaptic terminal
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Botulinum decreases ACh (blocks release), organophosphates increase ACh (block breakdown) — opposite mechanisms, both causing weakness
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Botulinum blocks ACh release (↓ACh → flaccid paralysis); organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase (↑↑ACh → overstimulation/depolarising block) — opposite mechanisms.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A non-depolarising neuromuscular blocker works by which mechanism?
options: Competitively antagonising the nicotinic receptor (no depolarisation)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Competitively antagonising the nicotinic receptor (no depolarisation)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Non-depolarising blockers (e.g. rocuronium) competitively antagonise the nicotinic receptor, preventing depolarisation.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient with myasthenia gravis becomes more weak. Distinguishing a myasthenic from a cholinergic crisis matters because they represent:
options: Too much vs too little calcium
Too little ACh (myasthenic) vs too much ACh (cholinergic) — both cause weakness
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Too little ACh (myasthenic) vs too much ACh (cholinergic) — both cause weakness
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: A myasthenic crisis is too little ACh effect, a cholinergic crisis (e.g. over-treatment) is too much ACh — both cause weakness and must be distinguished.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which cells resorb (break down) bone, and from which lineage do they arise?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Osteoclasts; monocyte/macrophage (haematopoietic) lineage
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb bone and arise from the monocyte/macrophage (haematopoietic) lineage ('osteoClasts Consume').

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A postmenopausal woman sustains a fragility fracture of the hip. Her bone has reduced mass but normal mineralisation. What is the diagnosis and the key mechanism?
options: Osteoporosis; loss of oestrogen leading to unrestrained osteoclast resorption
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Osteoporosis; loss of oestrogen leading to unrestrained osteoclast resorption
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation causing fragility fracture is osteoporosis; menopausal oestrogen loss removes the restraint on osteoclasts.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient with vitamin D deficiency has soft, poorly mineralised bones with bone pain. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Osteomalacia
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Reduced mineralisation from vitamin D deficiency, giving soft bone with pain, is osteomalacia (rickets in children).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: What is the key distinction between osteoporosis and osteomalacia?
options: Osteoporosis = reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation; osteomalacia = poorly mineralised (soft) bone from vitamin D deficiency
Both conditions are characterised by poor mineralisation of an otherwise normal bone mass
Osteomalacia is characterised by an increased bone mass with normal mineralisation
They are the same condition described at different ages of presentation
Osteoporosis is caused by vitamin D deficiency and osteomalacia by oestrogen loss
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Osteoporosis = reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation; osteomalacia = poorly mineralised (soft) bone from vitamin D deficiency
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Osteoporosis is too little (normally mineralised) bone; osteomalacia is poorly mineralised soft bone from vitamin D deficiency — different problems.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: How does chronically elevated PTH (e.g. in hyperparathyroidism or CKD) affect bone?
options: It builds bone, which is why recombinant PTH is used as an osteoporosis drug
It has no meaningful effect on bone, acting only on the kidney and the gut
It increases osteoclast resorption, causing bone loss as the body sacrifices the skeleton to maintain blood calcium
It improves mineralisation of newly laid osteoid, increasing bone density over time
It directly inhibits osteoclasts, which is why hyperparathyroidism protects the skeleton
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: It increases osteoclast resorption, causing bone loss as the body sacrifices the skeleton to maintain blood calcium
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Chronically high PTH drives osteoclastic resorption to raise blood calcium, causing bone loss.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: An elderly man has bone pain, an enlarged deformed skull and a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Paget's disease of bone
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Disordered excessive remodelling with deformity and markedly raised ALP is Paget's disease of bone.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which drug class is first-line for osteoporosis and works by inhibiting osteoclasts?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Bisphosphonates (e.g. alendronate)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts to reduce resorption and are first-line for osteoporosis (also used in Paget's and hypercalcaemia).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: According to Wolff's law, what happens to bone with weight-bearing exercise?
options: Bone remodels along lines of stress, so weight-bearing exercise builds bone
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Bone remodels along lines of stress, so weight-bearing exercise builds bone
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Wolff's law states bone remodels to mechanical load, so weight-bearing exercise builds bone.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which hormone restrains osteoclasts, such that its loss causes postmenopausal osteoporosis?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Oestrogen
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Oestrogen restrains osteoclasts; its loss at menopause causes unrestrained resorption and postmenopausal osteoporosis.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: In chronic kidney disease, which sequence leads to renal osteodystrophy?
options: Increased vitamin D activation leading to hypercalcaemia and bone loss
Excess oestrogen production driving accelerated osteoclastic bone loss
Reduced vitamin D activation + phosphate retention → secondary hyperparathyroidism → bone resorption
Reduced PTH secretion leading to under-resorption and brittle sclerotic bone
Excess calcitonin secretion producing progressively softened, undermineralised bone
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Reduced vitamin D activation + phosphate retention → secondary hyperparathyroidism → bone resorption
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Failing kidneys reduce 1-α-hydroxylation and retain phosphate, driving secondary hyperparathyroidism and bone resorption (renal osteodystrophy).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which monoclonal antibody reduces osteoclast formation by targeting RANKL?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Denosumab
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that reduces osteoclast formation.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which drug is recombinant PTH that, given intermittently, paradoxically builds bone (anabolic)?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Teriparatide
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Teriparatide is recombinant PTH; intermittent dosing has an anabolic (bone-building) effect.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which components give bone its properties: flexibility versus hardness?
options: Hydroxyapatite provides the flexibility and collagen provides the hardness
Both properties come from calcitonin acting on the mineral phase of bone
Trabecular bone provides hardness and cortical bone provides flexibility
Collagen provides flexibility/tensile strength; hydroxyapatite (calcium/phosphate) provides hardness and the calcium store
Neither component contributes materially to the mechanical strength of bone
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Collagen provides flexibility/tensile strength; hydroxyapatite (calcium/phosphate) provides hardness and the calcium store
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Collagen (organic) gives flexibility/tensile strength; hydroxyapatite (mineral) gives hardness/compressive strength and stores calcium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A raised alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate most likely reflects which process?
options: High bone turnover (e.g. Paget's, osteomalacia, bone metastases)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: High bone turnover (e.g. Paget's, osteomalacia, bone metastases)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: ALP is a marker of high bone turnover, rising in Paget's disease, osteomalacia and bone metastases.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient hyperventilates during a panic attack and develops perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm, but the total serum calcium is normal. What is the mechanism?
options: Hypercalcaemia produced by the stress response during the panic attack
Hyperkalaemia from the muscular activity of the hyperventilation itself
Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, lowering IONISED calcium and causing tetany
Low magnesium alone, independent of any change in the calcium level
Reduced sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release from the respiratory alkalosis
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, lowering IONISED calcium and causing tetany
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Respiratory alkalosis raises calcium binding to albumin, reducing ionised calcium and causing tetany despite a normal total calcium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which statement about blood calcium and neuromuscular excitability is correct?
options: Low calcium causes weakness; high calcium causes tetany
Calcium has no effect on excitability
High calcium causes seizures from hyperexcitability
Low calcium causes tetany (more excitable); high calcium causes weakness (less excitable)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Low calcium causes tetany (more excitable); high calcium causes weakness (less excitable)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Calcium stabilises the membrane, so low calcium → hyperexcitable (tetany) and high calcium → hypoexcitable (weakness) — the counterintuitive rule.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient develops carpopedal spasm, perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek's sign after a total thyroidectomy. What is the cause?
options: Hypercalcaemia from inadvertent parathyroid stimulation during surgery
Hypocalcaemia from parathyroid damage, causing neuromuscular hyperexcitability (tetany)
Hyperkalaemia from tissue injury sustained during the neck dissection
Malignant hyperthermia triggered by the volatile anaesthetic agent used
A respiratory alkalosis alone, with a normal ionised calcium throughout
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Hypocalcaemia from parathyroid damage, causing neuromuscular hyperexcitability (tetany)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Parathyroid damage during thyroidectomy causes hypocalcaemia, which increases neuromuscular excitability and causes tetany.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: The calcium that directly triggers skeletal muscle contraction comes from which source?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (intracellular store)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Skeletal muscle contraction is triggered by calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum — a pool separate from blood calcium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient with hypercalcaemia of malignancy presents with muscle weakness, lethargy and hyporeflexia. Why does high calcium cause these features?
options: It stabilises the membrane, making nerve/muscle less excitable (hypoexcitable)
It overloads the sarcoplasmic reticulum, exhausting the calcium stores
It blocks troponin C, preventing the thin filament from being activated
It depletes cellular ATP, so the contractile apparatus cannot be powered
It causes a metabolic alkalosis, which itself produces weakness and lethargy
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: It stabilises the membrane, making nerve/muscle less excitable (hypoexcitable)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: High blood calcium stabilises the membrane, raising the firing threshold and reducing excitability → weakness and hyporeflexia.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Approximately what proportion of the body's calcium is stored in bone, and in what form?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: About 99%, as hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: About 99% of body calcium is stored in bone as hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate).

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Why does chronically elevated PTH lead to bone loss?
options: It builds bone, which is why hyperparathyroidism raises bone density
It has no effect on bone, acting only on the kidney and the gut to raise calcium
It acts only on the kidneys, and the bone changes are an unrelated coincidence
It increases mineralisation of osteoid, which stiffens and then fractures the bone
Maintaining blood calcium takes priority, so PTH resorbs bone to release calcium — the skeleton is sacrificed
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Maintaining blood calcium takes priority, so PTH resorbs bone to release calcium — the skeleton is sacrificed
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Blood calcium takes priority over the skeleton, so chronic PTH drives bone resorption to defend blood calcium, causing bone loss.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: When interpreting a serum calcium result, why is it corrected for albumin?
options: Albumin stores calcium in bone and releases it when the level falls
Because the physiologically active fraction is ionised calcium; low albumin lowers total but not ionised calcium
Because albumin raises the ionised calcium and so masks a true hypercalcaemia
To detect hyperventilation, which alters the measured total calcium directly
It is not necessary — the total calcium is the physiologically active fraction
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Because the physiologically active fraction is ionised calcium; low albumin lowers total but not ionised calcium
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: The active fraction is ionised calcium; low albumin gives a low total but normal ionised calcium, so total calcium is corrected for albumin.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which pool of calcium is affected by blood calcium disorders (hypo/hypercalcaemia)?
options: Extracellular calcium, altering neuromuscular excitability (not the contraction machinery directly)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Extracellular calcium, altering neuromuscular excitability (not the contraction machinery directly)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Blood calcium disorders affect extracellular calcium and hence neuromuscular excitability; the intracellular SR contraction pool is separate.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: A patient with severe hypocalcaemia is at risk of which life-threatening features?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Laryngospasm and seizures (from neuromuscular hyperexcitability)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Severe hypocalcaemia causes marked neuromuscular hyperexcitability, risking laryngospasm and seizures.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which two roles of calcium in bone can come into conflict?
options: Its role in muscle contraction and its role in membrane excitability
Its absorption in the gut and its excretion by the kidney under PTH control
Its structural role (hardness) and its reservoir role (releasing calcium to maintain blood levels)
Its storage inside the cell and its storage within the mitochondria of the cell
None of these roles conflict, because bone calcium is metabolically inert
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: Its structural role (hardness) and its reservoir role (releasing calcium to maintain blood levels)
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: Bone's structural role (hydroxyapatite for strength) conflicts with its reservoir role, as calcium is drawn from bone to defend blood calcium.

conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.question: Which hormones maintain blood calcium in the narrow range needed for normal neuromuscular excitability?
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.answer: PTH and vitamin D
conditions__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Foundati.explanation: PTH (raises calcium by bone resorption, renal reabsorption and vitamin D activation) and vitamin D (gut absorption) keep blood calcium tightly controlled.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 58-year-old man presents with a sudden hot, swollen, painful first metatarsophalangeal joint. Aspiration is performed and fluid sent to the lab. Which microscopy finding confirms the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rhomboid crystals that are positively birefringent
Needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent, yellow when parallel to the compensator
Needle-shaped crystals that are positively birefringent
No crystals with a normal white cell count
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: Needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent, yellow when parallel to the compensator
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: Podagra (first MTP) with needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals (yellow when parallel to the red compensator axis) confirms gout. Rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals would indicate pseudogout; Gram-positive cocci would indicate septic arthritis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 76-year-old woman with an acutely hot, swollen knee has an aspirate showing rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals. Which additional finding or association most fits this diagnosis?
options: Podagra affecting the first MTP joint
Serum urate markedly elevated as the diagnostic test
Thiazide diuretic as the classic precipitant
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: Rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals are calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD/pseudogout), classically affecting the knee/wrist with chondrocalcinosis on X-ray and associated with older age, haemochromatosis and hyperparathyroidism. Podagra, tophi, diuretics and reliance on serum urate relate to gout.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 64-year-old man on diuretics has a hot, swollen, red knee and a fever of 38.5C. Aspiration shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose gout and discharge on colchicine, as crystals confirm the cause
Treat as possible septic arthritis: ensure Gram stain and culture were sent and start antibiotics after aspiration, alongside gout management
Wait for serum urate before making any decision
Start oral antibiotics only if the culture is positive at 48 hours
Give intra-articular steroid immediately as crystals exclude infection
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: Treat as possible septic arthritis: ensure Gram stain and culture were sent and start antibiotics after aspiration, alongside gout management
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: A crystal-positive result does NOT exclude coexisting septic arthritis — crystals and infection can occur together. A hot, swollen joint with fever must be treated as septic until proven otherwise: send Gram stain/culture/cell count, aspirate before antibiotics, and do not let the crystals falsely reassure you.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of a hot, red, swollen and exquisitely tender right knee that she cannot bend. She is febrile at 38.6°C. What is the single most appropriate immediate investigation?
options: Start IV flucloxacillin and review in 24 hours
Urgent joint aspiration before giving antibiotics
Oral NSAIDs and outpatient rheumatology referral
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: Urgent joint aspiration before giving antibiotics
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: A hot swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Urgent aspiration is the key diagnostic step and should be done before antibiotics so that Gram stain and culture are not sterilised. Imaging and NSAIDs must not delay this; antibiotics are given after the joint (and blood) are sampled. Withholding aspiration for 24 hours risks rapid joint destruction.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 25-year-old man has a hot swollen ankle. Synovial fluid shows a WCC of 68,000/mm³ with 85% neutrophils, turbid appearance, and a NEGATIVE Gram stain. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The high neutrophil-predominant WCC still strongly indicates septic arthritis and it should be treated as such
The negative Gram stain excludes septic arthritis
A WCC of 68,000 is typical of osteoarthritis
Crystals must be present for this to be inflammatory
No antibiotics are needed until culture confirms an organism
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: The high neutrophil-predominant WCC still strongly indicates septic arthritis and it should be treated as such
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: A synovial WCC >50,000 with >75% neutrophils is highly suggestive of septic arthritis. The Gram stain is only ~50% sensitive, so a negative result does NOT exclude infection — treat empirically after cultures. This WCC is far above the OA range (<2,000). In a young sexually active adult, also consider Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 4-year-old boy refuses to bear weight on his left leg, holds the hip flexed and externally rotated, and has a temperature of 39°C. Bloods show raised WCC and ESR. Which tool best helps distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: The Kocher criteria (fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, raised ESR, raised WCC) estimate the probability of septic arthritis versus transient synovitis in a child's hip. This child meets multiple criteria, so septic arthritis must be excluded with urgent aspiration/orthopaedic input. Ottawa rules apply to ankle fractures, Wells to VTE, Centor to sore throat, and Alvarado to appendicitis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 58-year-old woman has a 6-month history of symmetrical pain and swelling of the small joints of both hands with 90 minutes of early-morning stiffness. A hand X-ray shows uniform joint-space loss at the MCP and PIP joints, marginal erosions, periarticular osteopenia and soft-tissue swelling, with the DIP joints spared. Which single feature most specifically points to rheumatoid arthritis rather than osteoarthritis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: Loss of joint space and soft-tissue swelling are non-specific. Marginal (juxta-articular) erosions are the hallmark of the erosive inflammatory arthritis of RA, and RA characteristically spares the DIP joints — the combination is far more specific than any single LESS feature. Subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes are features of OA (LOSS), not RA.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 66-year-old man has painful DIP and PIP swellings and pain at the base of the thumb. Which set of X-ray findings best fits his likely diagnosis?
options: Symmetrical MCP erosions with periarticular osteopenia
Asymmetrical joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
Uniform joint-space loss with soft-tissue swelling and DIP sparing
Periarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions at the wrist
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: Asymmetrical joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: DIP (Heberden's) and thumb-base (1st CMC) involvement is classic osteoarthritis. OA = LOSS: asymmetrical Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, subchondral Sclerosis and subchondral cysts. The other options describe RA (symmetrical MCP erosions, periarticular osteopenia, DIP sparing) or spondyloarthropathy (sacroiliitis, syndesmophytes).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 44-year-old woman has 8 weeks of symmetrical swelling of the MCP and PIP joints with prolonged morning stiffness. Her hand and wrist radiographs are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her that RA is excluded by the normal X-ray
Repeat the plain radiograph in 2 years
Refer urgently for early inflammatory arthritis assessment
Diagnose osteoarthritis and advise weight loss
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: Refer urgently for early inflammatory arthritis assessment
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: Early RA X-rays are frequently normal because erosions and osteopenia are late changes — a normal film does not exclude RA. With a suggestive inflammatory history she should be referred urgently; ultrasound/MRI can detect early synovitis and erosions, and there is a 'window of opportunity' in which early DMARD therapy prevents irreversible joint damage. Reassurance, deferral or an OA label would miss treatable disease.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of symmetrical pain and early-morning stiffness in the small joints of both hands. Examination shows soft swelling of several MCP and PIP joints. Plain radiographs of the hands are reported as normal. RF and anti-CCP are pending. Which investigation is most likely to confirm active synovitis at this stage?
options: Ultrasound with power Doppler of the hands
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: Ultrasound with power Doppler of the hands
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: In early RA, X-ray is frequently normal because erosions take months to develop. Ultrasound shows synovial hypertrophy and effusion, and power Doppler demonstrates increased vascularity indicating active synovitis. It is cheap, radiation-free and bedside, making it the best first-line imaging to confirm synovitis early. Repeat X-ray only delays diagnosis; DEXA and CT do not assess synovial inflammation; bone scintigraphy is non-specific.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: An MRI of the wrist in a patient with suspected early rheumatoid arthritis shows synovial enhancement and focal bone marrow oedema within the carpal bones, with no erosions visible on plain X-ray. What is the main significance of the bone marrow oedema finding?
options: It indicates avascular necrosis of the carpal bones
It is a pre-erosive change that predicts future erosions and is prognostic
It is a normal age-related finding of no significance
It represents established irreversible joint destruction
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: It is a pre-erosive change that predicts future erosions and is prognostic
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: Bone marrow oedema (osteitis) on MRI represents inflammatory infiltrate within bone and is a pre-erosive change that strongly predicts the development of future erosions. It is one of the most important prognostic MRI findings in RA and supports early aggressive DMARD therapy. It is not infection, AVN, a normal finding, or established destruction.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: Which statement best reflects the correct interpretation of a normal plain hand X-ray in a patient with a clinically inflammatory small-joint arthritis?
options: It reliably excludes rheumatoid arthritis and no further imaging is needed
It excludes active synovitis but not future erosions
It indicates the disease is in remission
It confirms the diagnosis is osteoarthritis rather than RA
It does not exclude active RA; USS or MRI should be used to detect early synovitis
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: It does not exclude active RA; USS or MRI should be used to detect early synovitis
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: A normal X-ray is common in early RA and does not exclude active disease. USS (power Doppler) and MRI reveal synovitis and early erosions much earlier, enabling early DMARD therapy within the window of opportunity. A normal X-ray does not exclude RA, indicate remission, or confirm osteoarthritis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 26-year-old man has 8 months of low back and buttock pain with >45 minutes of morning stiffness that improves with exercise and wakes him at night. Examination shows reduced lumbar flexion (positive Schober's test). Plain AP pelvis X-ray of the sacroiliac joints is reported as normal. Which is the most appropriate next imaging investigation?
options: Repeat the pelvic X-ray in 12 months
MRI of the sacroiliac joints with STIR/T2 fat-saturated sequences
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: MRI of the sacroiliac joints with STIR/T2 fat-saturated sequences
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: The history is classic inflammatory back pain in a young man. A normal X-ray does not exclude axial spondyloarthritis because radiographic sacroiliitis is a late change. MRI (STIR/T2 fat-sat) detects early active sacroiliitis as subchondral bone marrow oedema, part of the ASAS criteria, and is the correct next step. CT and bone scans are not first-line for early disease, and delaying with a repeat film misses the window for early treatment.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A lateral lumbar spine radiograph of a 40-year-old man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis shows thin vertical ossifications bridging adjacent vertebral bodies and loss of the normal anterior vertebral concavity. Which single term best describes the overall appearance?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: Vertical marginal syndesmophytes bridging vertebral bodies together with squaring (loss of anterior concavity) produce the bamboo spine of ankylosing spondylitis. Rugger-jersey spine is renal osteodystrophy; DISH has bulky flowing right-sided ossification with preserved SI joints; degenerative spondylosis produces horizontal asymmetric osteophytes; the Scottie dog is an oblique lumbar/pars anatomy sign.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 55-year-old man with a 25-year history of ankylosing spondylitis and a fused, rigid spine falls from standing height and now has severe new upper back pain but no neurological deficit. Plain thoracic spine radiographs are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Arrange CT (and/or MRI) of the spine because of high fracture risk
Reassure and discharge with simple analgesia
Prescribe a short course of oral steroids and review in clinic
Repeat plain films in two weeks
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: Arrange CT (and/or MRI) of the spine because of high fracture risk
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: An ankylosed 'bamboo' spine is brittle and can sustain an unstable transverse fracture after even minor trauma, with a high risk of spinal cord injury. Plain films frequently miss these fractures. New back pain after trauma in an AS patient mandates cross-sectional imaging (CT for the fracture, MRI for cord/soft tissue) rather than reassurance or repeat radiographs.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.question: A 45-year-old with a 6-week symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis has a negative rheumatoid factor. Which statement is correct?
options: A negative RF excludes rheumatoid arthritis
RF is highly specific for RA
A negative RF does not exclude RA; check anti-CCP and refer on clinical grounds
Anti-CCP is less specific than RF
No referral is needed unless RF becomes positive
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.answer: A negative RF does not exclude RA; check anti-CCP and refer on clinical grounds
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Infl.explanation: About 30% of RA is seronegative, so a negative RF does not exclude it. Anti-CCP is far more specific (~95%) and prognostic; a patient with a persistent inflammatory polyarthritis should be referred early regardless of RF, within the window of opportunity for DMARDs.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman has a DEXA scan. Her lowest T-score is −2.7 at the femoral neck. She has no history of fracture. Which is the most accurate classification of her bone status?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: A T-score of ≤ −2.5 defines osteoporosis on the WHO classification. It would only be 'severe/established' osteoporosis if she also had a fragility fracture, which she does not. Osteopenia is −1.0 to −2.5, and normal is ≥ −1.0. Osteomalacia is defective mineralisation, not a DEXA classification.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 34-year-old premenopausal woman is investigated for recurrent low-trauma fractures. Her DEXA report gives a Z-score of −2.6. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her, as the T-score is the only score that matters at her age
Diagnose primary osteoporosis and start a bisphosphonate immediately without further tests
Repeat the DEXA in 5 years with no other action
Ignore the result because DEXA cannot be interpreted under age 40
Investigate for a secondary cause of low bone density
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.answer: Investigate for a secondary cause of low bone density
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: In premenopausal women, younger patients and children the Z-score (age-matched reference) is used rather than the T-score. A low Z-score is unexpectedly low for age and should prompt a search for a secondary cause (e.g. steroids, coeliac disease, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, hypogonadism, myeloma) before labelling it primary osteoporosis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 72-year-old man sustains a wrist fracture after tripping and falling from standing height onto the pavement. A subsequent DEXA shows a T-score of −1.8. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?
options: Normal DEXA excludes osteoporosis, so no treatment is needed
This is a fragility fracture indicating osteoporosis; offer bone-protection treatment despite the T-score
Osteopenia only; repeat DEXA in 2 years and take no further action
The fracture is unrelated to bone health and needs no metabolic assessment
Start treatment only if the T-score falls below −2.5 on repeat scanning
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.answer: This is a fragility fracture indicating osteoporosis; offer bone-protection treatment despite the T-score
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: A fracture from low-energy trauma (a fall from standing height or less) is a fragility fracture, which signifies osteoporosis regardless of the DEXA result and warrants treatment. A T-score of −1.8 is technically osteopenic, but the clinical fragility fracture overrides this, so bone protection (calcium/vitamin D plus a bisphosphonate, with falls prevention) is indicated.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 62-year-old woman with coeliac disease presents with diffuse bone pain and difficulty rising from a chair. A pelvic radiograph shows narrow symmetrical lucent bands running perpendicular to the cortex across both pubic rami and the medial femoral necks. Which single radiological sign do these represent?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: Narrow, symmetrical lucent bands perpendicular to the cortex at the pubic rami and medial femoral neck are Looser's zones — unmineralised osteoid, the hallmark of osteomalacia, here in the context of malabsorption from coeliac disease. Rugger-jersey spine relates to renal osteodystrophy and a Codman triangle to aggressive bone tumours.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 58-year-old man with a waddling gait and proximal muscle weakness is being investigated for osteomalacia. Which set of biochemical results best fits the diagnosis?
options: Low vitamin D, low/normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal ALP, normal PTH
High calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH
Low calcium, high phosphate, low ALP, low PTH
High calcium, high phosphate, normal ALP, low PTH
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.answer: Low vitamin D, low/normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: Osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency gives low 25-OH vitamin D, low/normal calcium, low phosphate, a raised ALP and a raised PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism). Entirely normal biochemistry (option B) would point to osteoporosis. High calcium with high ALP and high PTH suggests primary hyperparathyroidism.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 2-year-old with delayed walking and bowed legs has a wrist radiograph. Which finding is most characteristic of rickets?
options: Cupping, fraying and widening of the metaphysis with a widened growth plate
Premature fusion of the growth plate
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.answer: Cupping, fraying and widening of the metaphysis with a widened growth plate
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: Rickets shows metaphyseal cupping, fraying and widening with a widened, indistinct growth plate, plus bowing of long bones (genu varum) and a rachitic rosary. Punched-out lesions suggest myeloma, and dense sclerotic bands suggest lead lines or healing rather than active rickets.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 16-year-old presents with several weeks of pain and swelling around the right knee. X-ray of the distal femur shows a metaphyseal lesion with a triangular spur of new bone at its margin and fine radiating spicules extending perpendicular to the cortex into an adjacent soft-tissue mass. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: A Codman triangle plus sunburst spiculation in the metaphysis around the knee of an adolescent is classic for osteosarcoma. Ewing sarcoma is diaphyseal with an onion-skin reaction; osteochondroma, GCT and simple bone cyst are benign lesions without aggressive periosteal reaction or soft-tissue mass.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 12-year-old has a painful mid-shaft femoral lesion with fever and raised inflammatory markers. X-ray shows a permeative diaphyseal lesion with multiple concentric parallel layers of periosteal new bone. Which radiological sign and diagnosis do these findings represent?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: Concentric multi-layered periosteal new bone is the onion-skin sign, classic for Ewing sarcoma: a diaphyseal tumour of children that can present with fever and raised inflammatory markers mimicking osteomyelitis. Sunburst/Codman favour osteosarcoma; ground-glass and sclerotic rims are benign features.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A patient is found to have a bone lesion with X-ray features suspicious for a primary sarcoma. After plain films, MRI and staging CT, what is the most appropriate next step regarding tissue diagnosis?
options: Immediate biopsy in the local emergency department
Excisional biopsy by the local orthopaedic team before referral
Refer to a specialist sarcoma centre for biopsy at that centre
Repeat the X-ray in 6 weeks and biopsy only if it grows
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.answer: Refer to a specialist sarcoma centre for biopsy at that centre
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: Biopsy of a suspected bone sarcoma must be planned and performed at the specialist sarcoma centre, because a poorly sited biopsy tract contaminates tissue planes and can compromise limb-salvage surgery. Local biopsy, delay, and empirical chemotherapy without histology are all inappropriate.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A patient has raised calcium, low phosphate and a raised PTH. Which condition does this bone profile indicate, and what is the next step?
options: Primary hyperparathyroidism — refer for parathyroid imaging ± surgery
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.answer: Primary hyperparathyroidism — refer for parathyroid imaging ± surgery
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: Raised Ca with low phosphate and an inappropriately raised PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism; confirm and refer for parathyroid imaging (sestamibi/ultrasound) ± parathyroidectomy. Osteomalacia and CKD-MBD both have low calcium; Paget’s has normal calcium with isolated raised ALP.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.question: A 72-year-old has an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphate and PTH, and bony pain. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone.explanation: Isolated raised ALP with an otherwise normal bone profile suggests Paget’s disease; an isotope bone scan (with X-rays) maps disease activity and extent. Symptomatic Paget’s is treated with a bisphosphonate.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A 26-year-old woman reports her fingers turning white then blue then red in the cold since her teens, symmetrically in both hands, with no ulcers or skin changes. Nailfold capillaroscopy shows regular, evenly spaced uniform hairpin loops and ANA is negative. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start oral prednisolone for suspected systemic sclerosis
Urgent vascular surgery referral for digital sympathectomy
Reassure and advise conservative measures (keep warm, avoid triggers)
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.answer: Reassure and advise conservative measures (keep warm, avoid triggers)
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: Young age, symmetry, absence of tissue damage, NORMAL capillaroscopy and negative ANA all indicate benign PRIMARY Raynaud's phenomenon. Management is conservative — reassurance, keeping warm and avoiding triggers (calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine if troublesome). Immunosuppression, iloprost and surgery are for severe secondary disease, and there is nothing here to suggest systemic sclerosis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A 52-year-old woman with a 1-year history of Raynaud's and puffy fingers undergoes nailfold capillaroscopy. Which set of findings would most strongly indicate secondary Raynaud's due to evolving systemic sclerosis?
options: Uniform hairpin loops with regular spacing
Increased capillary density with no haemorrhage
Complete absence of any visible capillaries in a healthy young person
Slightly tortuous loops with normal calibre and no dropout
Giant capillaries, microhaemorrhages and avascular dropout
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.answer: Giant capillaries, microhaemorrhages and avascular dropout
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: The "scleroderma pattern" — giant (dilated) capillaries, microhaemorrhages, and capillary loss/avascular areas with architectural disorganisation — is the hallmark of secondary Raynaud's and evolving systemic sclerosis. Uniform hairpin loops are normal, and mild non-specific tortuosity does not constitute the scleroderma pattern.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A 48-year-old man with new Raynaud's is found to have a scleroderma pattern on capillaroscopy and a positive anti-centromere antibody. Which associated diagnosis does this antibody most specifically suggest?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: Anti-centromere antibodies are strongly associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome). Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc. A scleroderma-pattern capillaroscopy with an SSc-specific antibody strongly predicts progression to definite systemic sclerosis, so this is secondary — not primary — Raynaud's.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A 72-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of new right-sided temporal headache, scalp tenderness when combing her hair, and pain in her jaw when chewing. ESR is 88 mm/hr and CRP is markedly raised. She has no visual symptoms. What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Arrange an urgent temporal artery biopsy and withhold treatment until the result is available
Request an MRI brain before starting any treatment
Prescribe high-dose NSAIDs and review in one week
Start high-dose oral prednisolone immediately and arrange urgent investigation
Start IV methylprednisolone and admit for emergency plasma exchange
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.answer: Start high-dose oral prednisolone immediately and arrange urgent investigation
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: This is classic GCA (age >50, new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, very high ESR/CRP). Treatment must never be delayed for investigations. Without visual symptoms, oral prednisolone 40–60 mg/day is appropriate; IV methylprednisolone is reserved for visual involvement. The biopsy remains positive for ~1–2 weeks after steroids, so it can be arranged after treatment starts.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A temporal artery duplex ultrasound is performed on a patient with suspected giant cell arteritis. Which finding most strongly supports the diagnosis?
options: A hypoechoic circumferential wall thickening (halo sign) that persists on compression
A brightly hyperechoic ring around the lumen that disappears on compression
Absent arterial flow with a normal vessel wall
A calcified atherosclerotic plaque narrowing the lumen
Increased vessel wall echogenicity with a normal wall thickness
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.answer: A hypoechoic circumferential wall thickening (halo sign) that persists on compression
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: The halo sign is a hypoechoic (dark) circumferential ring of inflammatory wall oedema around the lumen. When the halo remains as the artery is compressed by the probe (non-compressible artery / positive compression sign), this strongly indicates vasculitis. Hyperechoic calcified plaque reflects atherosclerosis, not GCA.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A temporal artery biopsy from a patient clinically diagnosed with GCA returns as normal, showing no inflammation. Inflammatory markers were very high and the patient had jaw claudication and a raised, tender temporal artery. What is the best interpretation?
options: The diagnosis of GCA is excluded and steroids should be stopped
The biopsy must be repeated on the contralateral side before any treatment decision
A negative biopsy does not exclude GCA because of skip lesions; continue treatment based on the clinical picture
The high ESR is more consistent with infection, so start antibiotics
The result confirms polymyalgia rheumatica rather than GCA
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.answer: A negative biopsy does not exclude GCA because of skip lesions; continue treatment based on the clinical picture
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: GCA inflammation is patchy with skip lesions, so a biopsy can sample an uninvolved segment and appear normal. A negative biopsy does not exclude GCA — the diagnosis is ultimately clinical, supported by inflammatory markers and imaging. With a convincing clinical picture and raised markers, treatment should continue.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A patient with vague arthralgia has a negative ANA. What does this most reliably tell you?
options: Systemic lupus erythematosus is very unlikely
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.answer: Systemic lupus erythematosus is very unlikely
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: ANA is a highly sensitive screen for SLE, so a negative ANA has a high negative predictive value and makes SLE very unlikely. A positive ANA is non-specific and would need reflex testing (dsDNA, ENA).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A 60-year-old presents with haemoptysis, an active urinary sediment with red-cell casts and rising creatinine; c-ANCA/anti-PR3 is positive. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Reassurance and repeat ANCA in 3 months
High-dose corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab
Oral antibiotics for a chest infection
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.answer: High-dose corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: This is a pulmonary–renal syndrome from ANCA-associated vasculitis (PR3/GPA). It is an emergency requiring urgent immunosuppression — high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab — alongside renal/respiratory support.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.question: A woman with Raynaud’s and skin tightening is anti-centromere positive (limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis). Which surveillance is most appropriate?
options: Annual echocardiography and pulmonary function tests for pulmonary hypertension
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.answer: Annual echocardiography and pulmonary function tests for pulmonary hypertension
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Conn.explanation: Limited cutaneous SSc (anti-centromere) carries a risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension, so annual echocardiography and PFTs are recommended. Anti-Scl-70 (diffuse) instead prompts HRCT/PFT surveillance for interstitial lung disease.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: An 82-year-old woman falls and has a shortened, externally rotated left leg. AP pelvis shows a complete, fully displaced intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck with a broken Shenton's line. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement)
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: This is a Garden IV (complete, fully displaced) intracapsular NOF fracture. Displacement disrupts the retrograde blood supply to the femoral head, giving a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union, so displaced intracapsular fractures (Garden III–IV) are treated with arthroplasty rather than fixation. A DHS is used for extracapsular (intertrochanteric) fractures. Undisplaced Garden I–II may be internally fixed.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 30-year-old man twists his ankle. Radiographs show a fibular fracture above the level of the syndesmosis with widening of the medial clear space and talar shift. Which classification and stability best describes this?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Weber C — unstable
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: The Weber system classifies the fibular fracture by its level relative to the syndesmosis: A below (stable), B at the level (variable), C above (syndesmosis disrupted, unstable). A fracture above the syndesmosis with medial clear space widening/talar shift is Weber C and unstable, typically requiring ORIF with possible syndesmotic fixation. Feel the proximal fibula to exclude a Maisonneuve injury.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 9-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand. Wrist X-ray shows a fracture line passing through the distal radial physis and extending into the metaphysis. Which Salter-Harris type is this, and what is the key concern?
options: Type I — through the physis only, low growth-arrest risk
Type II — physis into metaphysis, risk of growth arrest
Type III — physis into epiphysis, intra-articular
Type IV — across metaphysis, physis and epiphysis
Type V — crush of the physis, worst prognosis
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Type II — physis into metaphysis, risk of growth arrest
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: A fracture through the physis extending into the metaphysis (leaving a triangular metaphyseal Thurston-Holland fragment) is Salter-Harris type II — the commonest physeal fracture (SALTR: A = Above/metaphysis). All physeal fractures carry a risk of growth arrest, and this must be considered and followed up, though risk rises with higher grades (III–V, especially the crush type V).

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 22-year-old man attends the emergency department after falling onto his outstretched right hand while skateboarding. He has marked tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial loading of the thumb. Dedicated scaphoid-view radiographs are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge with simple analgesia
Apply a below-elbow backslab and discharge with no follow-up
Refer for immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Apply a scaphoid cast/splint and arrange repeat radiographs or MRI
Prescribe a wrist support and advise return only if symptoms persist beyond 6 weeks
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Apply a scaphoid cast/splint and arrange repeat radiographs or MRI
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness with a normal X-ray is a suspected occult scaphoid fracture. A normal film does not exclude a fracture, so the patient must be immobilised and re-imaged — MRI (most sensitive) or repeat radiographs at 10–14 days. Discharging without follow-up risks non-union and AVN.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A scaphoid fracture through which region carries the highest risk of avascular necrosis, and why?
options: Proximal pole, because the retrograde blood supply enters distally
Distal pole, because it is closest to the radial styloid
Scaphoid tubercle, because of high mechanical load
Waist, because it is the widest part of the bone
Distal pole, because the blood supply enters proximally
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Proximal pole, because the retrograde blood supply enters distally
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: The scaphoid is supplied in a retrograde fashion by branches of the radial artery entering distally. Proximal pole fractures interrupt this supply to the proximal fragment, giving the highest risk of avascular necrosis and non-union.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: When requesting radiographs for a suspected scaphoid fracture, which specific view best profiles the scaphoid to reveal a waist fracture?
options: Oblique view of the fifth metacarpal
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: PA in ulnar deviation
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: Dedicated 'scaphoid views' include a PA projection in ulnar deviation, which elongates and profiles the scaphoid and improves detection of a waist fracture line. Standard neutral views often foreshorten the bone and can miss the fracture.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 32-year-old man falls onto an outstretched hand and presents with a painful, swollen elbow. A lateral radiograph shows an elevated anterior fat pad (sail sign) and a visible posterior fat pad, but you cannot identify a definite fracture line. What is the most likely underlying injury?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Radial head fracture
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: In adults, the commonest occult intra-articular elbow fracture producing a fat pad sign without a visible line is a radial head fracture. The fat pads are displaced by the haemarthrosis. Supracondylar fractures are the paediatric equivalent, not the adult one.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: Which of the following statements about elbow fat pads on a lateral radiograph is correct?
options: A visible posterior fat pad is a normal finding in most adults
Any visible posterior fat pad indicates a joint effusion and is abnormal
A small anterior fat pad is always pathological
Fat pads are best assessed on the AP (anteroposterior) view
The sail sign refers to elevation of the posterior fat pad
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Any visible posterior fat pad indicates a joint effusion and is abnormal
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: The posterior fat pad is normally hidden within the olecranon fossa, so any visualisation is abnormal and signifies an effusion/haemarthrosis. A small anterior fat pad can be normal; the sail sign is elevation of the ANTERIOR fat pad; fat pads are assessed on the LATERAL view.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 6-year-old falls off monkey bars and has a displaced supracondylar fracture. Which single examination finding most specifically tests the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN)?
options: Sensation over the first dorsal web space
Ability to make an 'OK' sign (thumb IP and index DIP flexion)
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Ability to make an 'OK' sign (thumb IP and index DIP flexion)
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: The AIN (a branch of the median nerve) supplies flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus; inability to flex the thumb IP and index DIP joints (failure of the 'OK' sign) indicates AIN injury, classically threatened in supracondylar fractures. Web-space sensation/wrist extension test the radial nerve, finger abduction tests the ulnar nerve.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: An 82-year-old woman falls at home and attends ED with right groin pain and inability to weight-bear. The leg is not obviously shortened or rotated. AP pelvis and lateral hip radiographs are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange MRI of the hip to exclude an occult fracture
Discharge with analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy
Repeat plain hip X-ray in 10 days
Encourage mobilisation and review if pain persists
Request a DEXA scan to assess bone density
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Arrange MRI of the hip to exclude an occult fracture
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: A normal X-ray does not exclude a hip fracture in an elderly faller who cannot weight-bear.
