NICE/BOAST guidance requires further imaging, and MRI is the investigation of choice as it is the most sensitive — detecting the fracture line and marrow oedema within hours. Discharging or mobilising risks displacement of an occult NOF fracture.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A frail 79-year-old man with a suspected occult hip fracture and a normal X-ray has a permanent pacemaker that is not MRI-conditional, so MRI cannot be performed. What is the most appropriate alternative imaging?
options: Repeat X-ray with additional oblique views
No further imaging; mobilise as tolerated
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: CT of the hip
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: When MRI is unavailable or contraindicated within 24 hours, CT is the recommended alternative. CT is fast and widely available but can miss non-displaced or impacted fractures, so a negative CT with strong clinical suspicion may still warrant senior orthopaedic review or delayed MRI.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: Which single feature best explains why MRI is preferred over CT for detecting an occult neck-of-femur fracture in the first hours after injury?
options: MRI uses ionising radiation to highlight the fracture
MRI is quicker to perform than CT in the acute setting
MRI reliably shows the fracture only after 10–14 days
MRI is less affected by patient movement than CT
MRI detects bone-marrow oedema before any cortical disruption is visible
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: MRI detects bone-marrow oedema before any cortical disruption is visible
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: MRI (STIR/T1) shows bone-marrow oedema and the fracture line within hours of injury, before radiographic or even CT-visible cortical/trabecular changes appear. It uses no ionising radiation. CT and plain films depend on visible bony disruption, so they can miss undisplaced fractures early.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 34-year-old man with SLE on long-term prednisolone presents with 6 weeks of progressive right groin pain worse on weight-bearing. Plain radiographs of the pelvis are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: MRI of the hips
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: This patient has classic AVN risk factors (SLE, corticosteroids) with hip pain and a normal X-ray. MRI is the most sensitive and earliest test, detecting marrow oedema and the double-line sign at a pre-collapse stage when joint-preserving treatment is still possible. A normal X-ray does not exclude AVN, and CT, bone scan and DEXA are all less sensitive/appropriate here.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 46-year-old woman with a history of heavy alcohol use has an X-ray showing a thin subchondral lucent crescent beneath the articular surface of the femoral head, with early flattening but a preserved joint space. Which Ficat stage does this represent?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Ficat stage III
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: The crescent sign indicates subchondral collapse and, with head flattening but preserved joint space, defines Ficat stage III. Stage I is a normal X-ray with positive MRI; stage II is sclerosis/cysts without collapse; stage IV adds joint-space narrowing and secondary OA.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 52-year-old man with sickle cell disease is diagnosed with femoral-head AVN. Imaging shows crescent sign with flattening of the femoral head and early joint-space narrowing with secondary osteoarthritic change. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Total hip arthroplasty
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: The head has collapsed with secondary OA (Ficat III–IV), which is post-collapse disease. Joint-preserving options such as core decompression and bisphosphonates are only useful pre-collapse (Ficat I–II). Once the head is collapsed with OA, total hip arthroplasty is the definitive treatment.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 24-year-old man has a manipulation under sedation for an anterior shoulder dislocation. Before you send him home, which single finding, if newly present compared with the pre-reduction assessment, most requires urgent action?
options: Mild residual shoulder ache on movement
A small Hill-Sachs defect noted on the check film
Loss of sensation over the lateral deltoid (regimental badge area) that was intact before reduction
Restricted external rotation due to pain
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Loss of sensation over the lateral deltoid (regimental badge area) that was intact before reduction
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: New numbness over the regimental badge area indicates an axillary nerve deficit that has appeared since the pre-reduction baseline — a red flag requiring immediate re-assessment and senior review. A Hill-Sachs defect is a common associated finding, and pain/bruising/stiffness are expected. The value of the pre-reduction exam is precisely to detect a NEW post-reduction deficit.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 30-year-old is brought in after a high-energy knee dislocation that has spontaneously relocated. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and symmetrical. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with a knee brace and outpatient MRI
Reassure — palpable pulses exclude vascular injury
Apply a full plaster cylinder and repeat X-ray in 2 weeks
Assess ABPI and have a low threshold for CT angiography of the popliteal vessels
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Assess ABPI and have a low threshold for CT angiography of the popliteal vessels
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: A knee dislocation is a popliteal artery injury until proven otherwise. Palpable pulses do NOT exclude an intimal tear that can thrombose later, so ABPI and CT angiography are warranted. This is limb-threatening and requires urgent vascular assessment, not discharge or false reassurance.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A distal radius (Colles-type) fracture is manipulated and a below-elbow backslab applied. What does the post-reduction check X-ray primarily confirm, and what else must be documented alongside it?
options: It confirms bone density; document the patient's weight
It confirms restored volar tilt and radial length plus cast position; document the post-reduction neurovascular status compared with baseline
It confirms the patient's identity; document consent only
It confirms soft-tissue swelling; document analgesia given
It confirms fracture age; document tetanus status only
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: It confirms restored volar tilt and radial length plus cast position; document the post-reduction neurovascular status compared with baseline
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: The check film confirms adequate reduction (acceptable volar tilt, radial height/length, no residual displacement) and satisfactory cast moulding/position. It must be paired with a repeat neurovascular examination compared with the pre-reduction baseline, and the patient counselled about compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, worse on passive stretch) needing cast splitting.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 24-year-old man sustains a closed tibial shaft fracture in a football tackle and has a below-knee backslab applied. Six hours later he reports severe, escalating calf pain unrelieved by morphine and marked pain when his toes are passively extended. His dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and capillary refill is 2 seconds. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Reassure and continue regular opioid analgesia
Elevate the limb well above the level of the heart
Arrange an urgent CT angiogram of the lower limb
Split the backslab down to skin and urgently escalate for fasciotomy
Wait until distal pulses are lost before intervening
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Split the backslab down to skin and urgently escalate for fasciotomy
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch with intact pulses is classic early acute compartment syndrome — pulselessness is a late sign. The first steps are to relieve external constriction (split the cast to skin) and arrange urgent fasciotomy. Elevation above the heart reduces perfusion and worsens ischaemia; angiography and waiting for pulselessness both cause dangerous delay.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: An unconscious, ventilated polytrauma patient has a swollen, tense right leg following a crush injury. Because he cannot report symptoms, intracompartmental pressure is measured. His diastolic blood pressure is 70 mmHg and the anterior compartment pressure is 45 mmHg. Which finding best indicates the need for fasciotomy?
options: Absolute compartment pressure of 45 mmHg alone
Compartment pressure equal to systolic blood pressure
Serum creatine kinase within normal limits
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: A delta pressure of 25 mmHg
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: Delta pressure = diastolic BP − compartment pressure = 70 − 45 = 25 mmHg. A delta pressure <30 mmHg is the more reliable indication for fasciotomy because it accounts for the patient's perfusion pressure. Although the absolute pressure of 45 mmHg exceeds the 30–40 mmHg threshold, the delta pressure is the preferred criterion; a normal CK does not exclude the diagnosis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: Which statement about acute compartment syndrome is correct?
options: It is primarily a radiological diagnosis requiring MRI confirmation
The affected limb should be elevated well above the heart to reduce swelling
It is a surgical emergency and a largely clinical diagnosis requiring urgent fasciotomy
Paralysis and pulselessness are early, sensitive signs that should prompt diagnosis
A single normal compartment pressure reading reliably excludes the diagnosis
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: It is a surgical emergency and a largely clinical diagnosis requiring urgent fasciotomy
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency diagnosed clinically (pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are earliest). Paralysis and pulselessness are late signs. The limb should be kept at heart level, not elevated above it. A single normal pressure reading does not exclude the diagnosis in a suggestive limb — treat the patient, not the number.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.question: A 4-month-old (not yet mobile) has a spiral femoral fracture; the history is vague and changes. Alongside treating the fracture, what is the most appropriate action?
options: Discharge with a follow-up fracture-clinic appointment
Reassure the parents and give analgesia only
Repeat the X-ray in two weeks and review
Urgent safeguarding referral and a skeletal survey
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.answer: Urgent safeguarding referral and a skeletal survey
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Frac.explanation: A femoral fracture in a non-ambulant infant with an inconsistent history is a classic non-accidental injury red flag. Involve seniors/paediatrics, perform a skeletal survey to look for other/older fractures, document carefully and make an urgent safeguarding referral.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: A 45-year-old man feels a sudden 'kick' to the back of his ankle playing squash and cannot push off. Ultrasound of the Achilles is requested. Which USS finding would confirm a complete rupture?
options: Diffuse fusiform tendon thickening with increased Doppler flow
Bright echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing within the tendon
A hypo-/anechoic gap with retracted tendon ends that changes on dynamic ankle movement
An anechoic collection deep to the deltoid with bursal thickening
Normal fibrillar tendon echotexture throughout its length
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.answer: A hypo-/anechoic gap with retracted tendon ends that changes on dynamic ankle movement
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: A complete Achilles rupture shows an anechoic/hypoechoic gap between retracted tendon ends, best confirmed dynamically. Fusiform thickening with Doppler flow indicates tendinopathy; echogenic foci with shadowing suggest calcification; a collection deep to deltoid describes the shoulder/bursa, not the Achilles.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: A 60-year-old woman with painful osteoarthritic knees presents with acute onset of left calf pain and swelling. She is worried about a clot. Which statement about the likely ultrasound diagnosis is most accurate?
options: A Baker's cyst arises within the joint capsule of the hip
Ultrasound cannot distinguish a Baker's cyst from a DVT
Baker's cysts never communicate with the knee joint
Anticoagulation should be started immediately without imaging
A ruptured Baker's cyst can mimic a DVT, so venous Doppler must be performed to exclude thrombus
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.answer: A ruptured Baker's cyst can mimic a DVT, so venous Doppler must be performed to exclude thrombus
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: A ruptured Baker's cyst (gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa, often communicating with the knee) causes acute calf pain/swelling mimicking DVT ('pseudothrombophlebitis'). USS reliably distinguishes the two, and DVT must be excluded before treating the cyst; anticoagulation should not be started blindly.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: A 58-year-old painter has chronic shoulder pain and weakness on abduction. Ultrasound is chosen as first-line imaging. Which is the strongest justification for USS over MRI here?
options: USS gives superior visualisation of bone marrow oedema
USS is dynamic and radiation-free and is validated for assessing superficial rotator-cuff tendons, allowing impingement to be seen during abduction
USS is unaffected by operator experience
USS is the best modality for deep intra-articular labral tears
MRI cannot detect full-thickness supraspinatus tears
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.answer: USS is dynamic and radiation-free and is validated for assessing superficial rotator-cuff tendons, allowing impingement to be seen during abduction
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: The rotator cuff is superficial, so USS is an excellent, radiation-free, dynamic first-line test able to show tears, calcific tendinitis, bursitis and impingement during movement. It is operator-dependent, and MRI remains superior for deep/intra-articular structures and marrow — so the other options are incorrect.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a non-healing plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head. On probing, the base feels hard and the probe reaches bone. Plain X-ray of the foot is reported as normal. CRP is elevated. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: A probe-to-bone-positive, non-healing diabetic foot ulcer with raised CRP strongly suggests osteomyelitis. A normal X-ray does not exclude it because plain-film changes are late (~10–14 days). MRI is the most sensitive and specific test, showing bone marrow oedema (low T1, high T2/STIR) and any deep collection or sinus tract, and it defines the extent for surgical planning.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: On an MRI performed for suspected early osteomyelitis, which signal pattern of the bone marrow is the characteristic early finding?
options: Low signal on T1, high signal on T2/STIR
High signal on T1, low signal on T2/STIR
High signal on both T1 and T2
Low signal on both T1 and T2
No change in marrow signal until 2 weeks
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.answer: Low signal on T1, high signal on T2/STIR
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: Infection replaces normal fatty marrow with oedema and inflammatory cells. Fat is bright on T1, so its loss produces low T1 signal, while the increased water content produces high signal on T2 and fat-suppressed STIR sequences. This bone marrow oedema is the earliest MRI sign and appears well before any X-ray change.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: A 64-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of worsening thoracic back pain, fever, and markedly raised CRP and ESR. Overnight he develops bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention. Which complication must be excluded most urgently?
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: The picture is vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis (back pain + fever + raised markers). New bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention indicate cord compression from an epidural abscess — a surgical emergency. Urgent whole-spine MRI with contrast is required to identify the collection and disc/endplate involvement and to guide decompression.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: A 24-year-old man reports 8 months of lower back pain and stiffness that is worst in the early morning, lasts about an hour, and eases with exercise. On the spine component of a GALS screen you perform a modified Schober's test: marks are placed 10 cm above and 5 cm below the lumbosacral junction. On maximal forward flexion the distance between the marks increases from 15 cm to 18.5 cm. Which single statement best interprets this finding?
options: The test is normal because the distance increased by more than 2 cm
The finding is diagnostic of lumbar disc prolapse
The test is invalid because the lower mark should be 10 cm below
Reduced flexion here confirms mechanical back pain and needs no further work-up
Lumbar flexion is reduced, consistent with axial spondyloarthritis
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.answer: Lumbar flexion is reduced, consistent with axial spondyloarthritis
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: A normal modified Schober's increases by more than 5 cm on flexion (15 cm to >20 cm). Here the increase is only 3.5 cm (15 to 18.5), so lumbar flexion is reduced. Combined with inflammatory back pain features (young man, morning stiffness >30 min, improves with exercise), this should prompt an axial spondyloarthritis work-up with MRI SI joints and HLA-B27 — not reassurance. The marks are correctly placed at +10/−5 cm, and the test does not diagnose disc prolapse.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: A final-year student is asked to explain the purpose of the GALS screen. Which single statement is the most accurate?
options: It is a full regional examination that replaces the need for REMS
It is a rapid screen to detect significant MSK disease and flag who needs a focused regional exam
It is used only to diagnose ankylosing spondylitis
It should only be performed in patients presenting with an obvious swollen joint
A normal GALS excludes all forms of musculoskeletal pathology with certainty
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.answer: It is a rapid screen to detect significant MSK disease and flag who needs a focused regional exam
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: GALS (Gait, Arms, Legs, Spine) is a quick screening tool, not a definitive regional examination. It is intended for patients without an obvious regional problem and identifies who needs a focused Regional Examination of the Musculoskeletal System (REMS). A normal screen makes significant disease unlikely but does not exclude all pathology, and it is not specific to any single diagnosis such as ankylosing spondylitis.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: During the Legs component of a GALS screen on a 60-year-old woman, you flex the knee and hip and note coarse crepitus and a positive patellar tap. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her that GALS is normal and discharge
Immediately request MRI of the sacroiliac joints
Repeat the three screening questions and take no further action
Proceed to a focused regional examination (REMS) of the knee
Diagnose septic arthritis and start IV antibiotics without further assessment
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.answer: Proceed to a focused regional examination (REMS) of the knee
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: A positive patellar tap indicates a knee effusion and crepitus suggests joint pathology — these are abnormal GALS findings. GALS is only a screen, so any abnormality warrants a focused regional examination (look, feel, move, special tests) of the affected joint, here the knee, followed by targeted investigation. MRI SI joints relates to axial spondyloarthritis, not this presentation, and neither discharge nor empirical antibiotics is justified on screening findings alone.

investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.question: Ultrasound of a swollen wrist shows synovial hypertrophy with increased power Doppler signal and small marginal erosions. What does this indicate and what is the next step?
options: Active synovitis — enter the inflammatory arthritis pathway
A tendon tear — refer to orthopaedics
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.answer: Active synovitis — enter the inflammatory arthritis pathway
investigations__MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Ultr.explanation: Synovial hypertrophy with power Doppler signal indicates active synovitis, and USS-detected erosions appear before plain-film changes; this routes the patient into the inflammatory arthritis pathway for serology and DMARD assessment.
